maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
On behalf of Mr. Fielding I beg to introduce Bill (No.

50) respecting banks and banking which appears in his name on the Order Paper. The charters of our banks will expire on the first of July next and it becomes necessary to have a new Banking Act passed this session. In the absence of the Minister of Finance I beg to introduce the Bill now, so that it may be printed and gotten ready for distribution, so that the House and the country may take communication of it, and that we may be ready to consider it when we meet again after the Christmas holidays. The Bill which I am presenting is practically the same as the law now in existence. The changes are not many and with the exception of one or two are not of very great consequence. The most important feature which is introduced into this Bill is that it contains a section which provides that at a general meeting of the shareholders they can appoint auditors of their own to have the affairs of the bank specially audited, and, if the shareholders choose to do so at any time thereafter a proportion of the shareholders representing five per cent of the capital of the bank can ask for the appointment of such auditors. These auditors will have power to inspect the company's books, to have access to them, to ask for information necessary and to compel it to be furnished, and their report is to be included in the annual statement presented to the shareholders.

maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is no provision for bank inspection?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That would meet the case which arose at the annual meeting of the Bank of Montreal the other day when certain shareholders asked for information and were denied it. Under this provision in the Bill they would probably get that information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
They would certainly get it under this clause. The shareholders representing five per cent of the capital can at any time ask the Bankers' Association to have such an audit made, and the report of the audit is to be included in the annual statement presented to the shareholders. I understand that this provision is taken from the existing law in England with regard to joint stock banks. Another feature which is new legislation, is, and it may be of some importance, that the annual statement cannot be signed by the president alone, but must be signed by three directors of the bank also. Another new feature in the Bill is a provision that the annual reports and statement of accounts, and the documents issued by the bank must be issued upon the authority and signature of the proper officers, upon whom if they do not acquaint themselves by actual information of the truth of what
they sign the civil and criminal liability rests. It would not be sufficient for these officials to say that they had signed in good faith as was done in former days, but every official of a bank whatever his rank or standing who under the law is compelled to put his signature to a document must personally acquaint himself as to the truth of the facts therein contained, and he becomes responsible.

maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Do I understand that the signature of the president and three directors must be attached to the monthly sworn statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Only just to the annual statement to the shareholders?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BANKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Yes. The new feature is that when statements and documents are issued by the bank under the law, the officer signing is liable if he fails to acquaint himself by actual verification of the truth of the statement to which he appended his signature and he is responsible for it civilly and criminally. A new feature of the Bill to which I call attention is in regard to the organization of a bank. In order to remind the shareholders or intending subscribers that they are subject to the double liability it is provided that all the documents which are issued in connection with the formation of a bank shall have printed on them, the section of the law which provides for the double liability of the shareholders. It is not a matter of very great importance, but the object is to remind shareholders at all t'mes that the moment they become shareholders they are liable to the double liability. Another provision of the Bill is that if the promoters fail to organize a bank then the money paid in has to be returned to the subscribers without any deduction for promotion fees or any other expense except what is allowed by the subscribers themselves. Then, some of the old banks have their shares fixed at $50 each instead of $100 and if they want to make their shares $100 each, which is now the usual parity, they cannot do it except by special legislation. There is machinery provided in this Bill that this can be done by resolution of the shareholders. Another new provision in the Bill is as to the products of the forest which may be tendered as security to the banks, and it provides that they shall include saw-logs and railway ties as timber, and deals, boards and staves as other lumber. This we conceived was always the intention, but a decision has recently been given in a court of justice that this covers only the products of the forest as they come from the forest, that they cease to have that character the moment they undergo some process of manufacture. The object of the

amendment is to make this clear and nothing else.
A new feature is that power is given to the receiver of an insolvent bank to borrow money under certain restrictions.
These are the main features of the Bill; the others are so minor that they will not require any explanation on my part.

maintopic: FISHERIES ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
Mr. BARNARD moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 58) to amend the Fisheries Act. He said: This Bill provides that salmon fishing gill net licenses shall not be issued on the Pacific coast to men who are not able to come up to the physical standard required by the regulations in force with respect to enlistment in the naval militia. Section 54 of the Fisheries Act provides that the minister shall have the right to make regulations for the issue of licenses. One of these regulations is as follows:
No license shall be granted to any person, company or firm unless such person is a British subject, resident in the province of British Columbia, or to such company or firm, unless it is a Canadian company or firm, or is licensed to do business in British Columbia.
I propose to amend this regulation by requiring that the licensee shall come up to the physical standard required of candidates for enlistment in the naval militia. Four thousand gill-net licenses are issued annually on that coast. Professor Prince, in his report for 1906, stated that 85 per cent of the licensees on the Fraser river were Japanese. It is well known that the Japanese are a small and undersized race, and in the event of this Bill becoming law the greater portion of these Japanese, who have heretofore taken out licenses, will no longer be able to obtain them, thus restoring the industry to our own people. In addition, a fishing population will be created on that coast from whom the government will be able to draw recruits for the naval service, a condition that does not obtain to-day.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: NORTHWEST SCHOOL LANDS.

speechtext:
Mr. McCarthy :
1.	Are school lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta only disposed of by public competition?
2.	What is the complete procedure followed by the government in order to determine the desirability of offering such lands for sale?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: NORTHWEST SCHOOL LANDS.
speechtext:
1.	School lands in the province of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are only 43
disposed of by sale at public auction except in cases where application is made by railway companies to acquire school lands for right-of-way, station grounds and other similar purposes of the railway, in which oases the land required for these purposes is disposed of to the company under the provisions of the Railway Act, that is to say, on such terms as the Governor in Council may prescribe, the practice being to have the land applied for inspected and valued by an officer of the department -and then to seek the consent of the Governor in Council for the sale of the land required for the purpose mentioned at the price determined on, and also in cases where application is made by boards of trustees to acquire the land necessary for school sites in school sections. In such cases upon the application of the trustees being endorsed by the Minister of Education for the province in which the land is situated, the land, not exceeding four acres, is sold to the board at the minimum price provided by the Dominion Lands Act in such cases, namely $10 per acre.
2.	All applications to have school lands offered for sale are referred to the superintendent of school lands, Winnipeg, who, after investigation, reports whether or not he considers it would be in the interests of the School Lands Endowment Fund to offer the lands at public auction at the' time proposed, and at the same time suggests the places and dates of sale.
If his recommendation is approved by the department the consent of the Governor General in Council is then sought and upon it being obtained a list of the undisposed of lands in the district referred to is furnished the superintendent of school lands, who then has such lands inspected and valued for the purpose of determining the upset price in each case.
It is also the practice before holding an auction sale of school lands to consult the government of the province in which the lands are situated and to submit to the Department of Public Works of that province a list of the lands to be offered so that it may notify this department of any reservations necessary for public roads or other purposes, and for any remarks that may be considered necessary.

COMMANDER ROPER.
speechtext: I desire to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to an answer he gave to a question asked by me the other day; and in this connection I might draw his attention to the fact that the officers in his department show very little care in preparing these answers. The question I put was:-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: COMMANDER ROPER.
speechtext:
Is the government aware that the latest and best English dictionaries define the word ' faction ' as always used in an opprobrious sense ?
The hon. minister replied that Commander Roper had used the word, not in the way in which we poor Canadian habitants use it, but as it is used in England.: It was on this account that I put the question I have just read, and I got this reply :-
The minister has asked Commander Roper to define the sense in which the word ' faction ' was used by him in the speech referred to by the hon. member. He is informed by Commander Roper that he used the word 'faction' meaning a large number of persons, and did not in any way attach any opprobrious sense to the word.
Neither the hon. minister nor anybody else will find any such definition in any English dictionary in England or elsewhere. I also put the further question:-
Was it intimated to Commander Roper by the deputy Minister of Marine that he should deliver himself of the ' faction ' address during the past autumn on the occasion referred to in the debate from which the foregoing extract is taken.
The minister's answer was entirely wide of the mark. He said that:-
Commander Roper delivered an address last fall at the Central Canada exhibition at the invitation of the directors of that exhibition.
But what I wanted to know was who inspired the directors to ask this officer to deliver that address. In other words, was it arranged by the minister or his deputy that the address should be given in order that this ' faction ' speech might be delivered to the country. The answer given was therefore not an answer to my ques-. tion at all. Then I asked:-
W as the address or were the notes of the same talked over by the deputy minister and Commander Roper before said delivery.
In reply the minister admitted that they were, but he made the admission very awkwardly. What he said was:-
The deputy minister knew that Commander Roper was to deliver an address at the Central Canada exhibition, explaining the organization of the Canadian navy from the point of view of the technical officer. The deputy minister and Commander Roper talked over some of the points of the address.
The hon. gentleman might just as well have told us that the whole thing was prepared by his deputy and Commander Roper; and he might have let us further know that the whole matter was submitted to him and he gave his approval.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
maintopic: COMMANDER ROPER.
speechtext:
I must say that the question which was put was quite a surprise to me, especially the way in which

it was drafted, and I was inclined to think that it was rather out of order. I do not think it is proper to ask the government what is the definition given in a dictionary. We are not here to discuss academic questions. But my hon. friend went further. He said that Commander Roper had delivered himself of a ' faction ' address. I do not think that he had any right to put a question implying anything of the kind.

maintopic: COMMANDER ROPER.
speechtext: I quoted Commander Roper's own words and put the inside quotation marks.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
maintopic: COMMANDER ROPER.
speechtext: When my hon. friend called it a ' faction ' address I could have taken exception, but I did nothing of the kind. I did give him an answer and gave it to the best of my knowledge and on the information supplied to me. The hon. gentleman asked whether these things were known to me, and I said no. To-day the hon. gentleman asks me whether it was arranged by myself with the exhibition committee that Commander Roper should be invited, and I tell him again, no; I never had anything to do with it,' and knew of this address delivered at the Canada Central exhibition only after it had been delivered.

maintopic: COMMANDER ROPER.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman, in answering a question of mine the other day, when asked if he knew of the speech, said: ' Certainly,' he knew the speech was going to be delivered.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
maintopic: COMMANDER ROPER.
speechtext: No, I never said that. I do not think the hon. gentleman can refer to any such statement of mine. If I am so reported, it is a mistake; I never said it. I did not know anything about the speech until after it was delivered.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MOLLOY.
PRIVILEGE-MR. MOLLOY.
speechtext:
In the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' of December 12,
appears the following, which I read because of its bearing on myself:
G.	H. Bradbury, member for Selkirk, continues to make things unpleasant for the Minister of Interior. Mr. Bradbury has asked a number of very pointed questions concerning the deal by which the St. Peter's Indians were tricked out of their land holdings in the reserve. The answers submitted by Mr. Oliver explain so little that Mr. Bradbury promptly put another rod in pickle. The matter will be found difficult of suppression, and it is understood that the Interior Department is preparing to meet Bradbury's charges as best it can. Mr. Bradbury, by the way, is one of the hardest workers in the House. I have not failed to see him in his seat at every session of the House. In this respect, Mr. Bradbury and the other Conservative members from Manitoba contrast to advantage with the two Liberal members from that province. Every time I have been in the press gallery, Mr. Sifton's seat has been either vacant or occupied by another member, and I haven't seen Dr. Molloy since I began my service in Ottawa.
Now, what are the facts in connection with this matter? The first man to whom I spoke on this subject was my good friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin). a Conservative, and a manly fellow-I have always found him so. I showed him the article, and he said that every member of the House knew that it was an untruth, and that he would help me to right the wrong that had been done me. He went with me to the office of the Auditor General. We first went to the accountant, and were advised by him to go to Mr. Gross. We saw Mr. Gross, who had my attendance and the cheque I had cashed for my attendance on the first session of this parliament, which, by the way, was cashed on May 27. I am under a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for South Cape Breton. I am under a debt of gratitude also to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe), who said: ' The statement is not true; your attendance has been as good as that of any man in the House.' And I am under a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) who said that it was not true and that it was unfair politics. And these gentlemen will make the same statement in the House that they made to me.
This parliament opened in January, 1909, and my record for attendance during that session is as follows:	In January I did
not miss one day. In February I missed one day: in March no days; in April no days. In May I drew my sessional indemnity on May 15, intending to go home then, but changed my plans and remained until the House closed on May .18. Having drawn my sessional indemnity on the 15th of May, the Auditor General's Department charged me with the loss of four days in May, 1909, but as a matter of fact

I stayed until the House prorogued. Last session the House opened in November, and I left for home five days before the Christmas holiday, and returned one day after the opening. This caused me to miss six days, and these were the only days missed by me during the whole session, and they were spent in my constituency. It will be seen that in the last two sessions of parliament I onlv missed seven days from actual attendance. This session, I have never missed a sitting, afternoon or evening.
I make that statement on my honour as a member of this House. If that statement is not true, I will leave this House and remain out of it. The statement in this newspaper, so far as it refers to me, is false. I cannot help but believe that it was not done unwittingly but was done designedly to injure me in my constituency. I remember a statement by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) during the first session of my membership in this House. That statement was : 'Play the game, but play it fair.' That is all I ask from the press of this country, whether Liberal or Tory, that is all I ask from hon. members on either side of this House; and I believe it is the duty of the man who wrote that article, to atone, at least in part, for the rank injustice he has tried to do me.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-ME. BEST.
PRIVILEGE-ME. BEST.
speechtext: I find a statement made in the St. John ' Daily Telegraph ' of Saturday, December 10, to the effect that I said there were thirty members of this House who had not paid for the printing of their speeches. I did not say that. In my remarks on December 9, I said that the Auditor General's Report showed that the Senate had paid several of their employees more than the statute allowed. And I say that now. And I say it is not right that money should be paid in that way. If a boy goes out and steals a loaf of bread, he is arrested and put in jail. Merely because men happen to have the position of law-makers, that does not give them the right to pay out the people's money in defiance of the law. I stated also that the Auditor General's Report showed that some of the members of this House had not paid for the printing of their speeches. And I make that statement to-day. It does not matter to me whether the members thus referred to are on this side or on the other side; if they have not paid for their speeches they ought to be required to pay for them. We are sent here to protect the public treasury. I asked if refunds had been made, and that question has not been answered yet. I merely wish to say that if the item in this newspaper went from any authority within the precincts of this House, I can only say that it is not correct, and that I did not make the statement attributed to me.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-ME. BEST.
QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.
speechtext:
(Translation). Mr. Speaker, before the orders ol the day are called, I deem it my duty to raise a question of privilege. Not only do I claim it as a right, but I deem it in my interest, before being put under the ban of public opinion in my constituency, to give some explanations, and to ask for certain corrections.
I would like to know the reason why I am reported in the unrevised edition of ' Hansard ', pages 1196-1197, of the 12th December, as having said that the electors of the county of Montmagny are less intelligent than the electors of other constituencies. I wish to state here that I stated just the reverse of what I am reported to have said. I may add that it would not be the part of an intelligent man to come down and state before this House that the electors who sent him here are not intelligent.
I wish to make these remarks because I have already received a letter from one of my constituents calling my attention to the above report. That is the reason why I should like ' Hansard ' to be corrected as follows: by replacing in the third line of the second paragraph of my remarks, the word, ' as ' by the word ' more ' Further, certain members of sentences have been cut off, the absence of which renders my remarks unintelligible. Therefore, I want those parts of sentences thus cut off to be added to the text. In the fifteenth line of the fourth paragraph, I should like the word ' serve ' to be substituted to ' would serve '.
Again, in the last line of the twelfth paragraph, I should like the words ' but not branch lines ' which cannot be understood by themselves, to be cut off, and replaced by the following, which I did really pronounce: ' But who have not yet been consulted on the question of branch lines to be built '.
Finally, in a last request I have to formulate is that, in order to make intelligible the last sentence of my speech, the following words be added: ' Should there be a deficit in the administration of that branch line '.
My object is not to throw blame on anybody, but to clearly define the position I have taken before the House.
It remains only for me, Sir, to beg the House's pardon for having spoken at such length, but I only wished to have the mistakes corrected which had crept into my speech.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS.
ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS.
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the House to a matter of sufficient public importance to demand a re-

ference to it. I placed on the Order Paper for December 5, the following question :-
1.	Wliat action, if any, has the government taken with a view to putting a stop to the use of His Majesty's mails for the * furtherance of get rich quick ' schemes, such as the one conducted by Mr. Sheldon in Montreal, and the numerous wild cat ventures that have been foisted on our people during the past few years?
2.	Has the government made any effort to prosecute the guilty parties?
The answer to that question was given by the right hon. the First Minister, and is" one to which I wish to take objection. He said:-
In the case of illegal lotteries, or schemes devised and intended to deceive the public for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretenses, the power of the department is limited to declaring correspondence relating to such schemes not to be mailable matter, and to refusing to deliver it.
Well, Sir, if the post office authorities have control only over the mailing matter that is delivered in this way, it is time that we appoint a public prosecutor, whereby such men as Mr. Sheldon may be prosecuted, and that others who are carrying on such work may be brought to justice. The answer further says:-
This power the department exercises in every case where it is proven to the satisfaction of the department that such a scheme is in * operation. The department has no power to institute a prosecution in such cases, but in all cases notifies the provincial authorities in whom are vested full powers of crininal prosecution.
I would like to ask the First Minister if any other department, such as the Department of Public Works, would be unable to bring action against any officer of that department who had made a misstatement in reference to the purchase of public domain, whether they would not be able to prosecute those parties? Is it not possible for any individual to demand that this matter should be investigated, and at the same time to take the present case into consideration?

I do not think that is very kind. I said to the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Barnard) the other day, when he asked for particulars of entries made by certain parties in the custom house and as to1 whether they had passed any goods free through the custom house, that I was afraid that he was asking for something that I was not able to give him. I did not make the law; the department did not make the law; parliament made the law by which it expressly declared that you must not reveal the contents of any invoice that passes through the customs only to the person who has made the entry, which information, if he demands it, he can have for fifty cents, but in no other case can he have it except upon an order of the court. Is the department to be blamed because it carries out the law that parliament enacted? I have no desire to withhold anything; we could give everything in the department that you want, but we must conform to the law. When the hon. gentleman was asking, the other day, for particular entries made by a certain gentleman I said that it was an unusual tiling to do, but this is a case which you are making inquiries about transactions between certain individuals and the departments of this government, and, that being the case, I thought I was warranted in giving the information. Parliament, I suppose, can do it, but where would you be if any man was at liberty to go and demand to see the invoices of another man? vVhat would be the result to trade if that could be done? I do not know what view my hon. friend would take of himself, but surely there is no business man in this House who would try to force the department to give the particulars of an individual's transaction that might be used against him. That is all I have to say. The answer was intended to be courteous, and I am sorry if the hon. gentleman thinks that it is not courteous. In the first place, I intimated to him that we could not give the information that he asks for short of weeks and weeks necessary to hunt it up, but we will do the very best we can. Some of the information that he asks for is confidential with reference to invoices and entries. Parliament has made

a law which says that we shall not reveal it, but if the House will assume the responsibility of saying to me that I shall reveal it, then I have no objection in the slightest.

If you want to know the valuation at which an article is admitted and how we arrive at that valuation, I would say that we arrive at it by the invoice of the parties who export the goods into this country ; and, of course, we would have to reveal in that case the invoice from the man who has sent the goods in, which the law says we shall not do.

maintopic: DUTIES ON AGRICULTURAL IMPLEMENTS.
speechtext: Has the minister made any refund in duties that have been collected on certain invoices to certain people?

maintopic: DUTIES ON AGRICULTURAL IMPLEMENTS.
speechtext:
Yes, we do so very often. We have to make amendments and
corrections to entries. If we have ascertained that goods have been entered at an incorrect valuation under the law we have to call upon the parties for an amended entry. If, on the other hand, we find that the parties have substantiated their claim that they have paid on the higher value than they ought to then a refund is handed to them. That is going on continually. It is not only in agricultural implements. There is nothing done by us with regard to agricultural implements that is not done with anything else. The invoice comes in from the exporter, it comes to the custom house, and it shows the figure at which the article is priced. In accordance with the custom law, appearing on that invoice is the price at which the article is disposed of under similar conditions in the United States. There is a certificate of the exporter himself attached to the invoice and we accept the invoice as being correct unless we have reason to think it is not correct. That is what is done and that is what has always been done.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.

speechtext: D.	SHELDON.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
Under rule 39 the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) asks for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing the illegal use of His Majety's mails. Under subsection 4 he has handed me this statement. Shall the hon. gentleman have leave to make the motion?
The House granted leave.
Mr. ARMSTRONG moved that the House do now adjourn. He said: I appreciate the privilege accorded me by the House and I believe the matter with which I shall deal is of sufficient importance to warrant a definite statement being made in regard to

it by the government. The First Minister in reply to a question which I placed on the Order Paper recently made the following statement:
' The department has no power to institute prosecution in such cases, but in all cases notifies the provincial authorities in whom are vested full powers of criminal prosecution.'
Now, applying this to the case of C. D. Sheldon we can see how justice may miscarry. This man Sheldon came to Canada two years ago from Boston where he had been a school teacher, and he settled in the city of Montreal, where he engaged in what is called blind-pool selling. The post office authorities, must have been aware, or they should have been aware, shortly after his arrival in Montreal, that he was carrying on a business which could not possibly be conducted in a legitimate way. To the Toronto ' Saturday Night' and the Montreal ' Star ' are due a great deal of credit for exposing Sheldon and his methods.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: What about the Montreal ' Herald '?

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
If the Solicitor General will take the trouble to read the files of the Montreal ' Herald ' he will find that there was sufficient in the articles published by that paper to encourage men to invest in this rascally work that was carried on by Sheldon. I cannot give to the Montreal ' Herald ' the credit which the hon. gentleman would like me to give. Not only newspapers, but a number of prominent men throughout the country have been instrumental in ferreting out these frauds. I can only mention Mr. Youel, of Aylmer, Ontario, who devoted months of his time previous to Sheldon's disappearance to exposing this man and his methods. I have here numbers of letters, some of them in the handwriting of Sheldon himself, making propositions that were so unreasonable and so unbusinesslike that any man could know that there was no other possible outcome than failure, and that the poor people of Canada would be fleeced as they have been fleeced. There is no doubt that Sheldon, who acted the part of a trepanner in this transaction, and his agents, his decoy men throughout the country, have been conducting a transaction which there is no language strong enough to condemn I have letters from the agents of Mr. Sheldon which have been sent to different persons in different parts of the country, some from his agents in the city of St. Thomas, where he is supposed to have taken over $200,000 of the people's money, and conducted his business, to some extent at least, by money which he received from that source. Any reasonable-minded man reading the letters from Sheldon's agents,
would know that the transactions he was carrying on in Montreal were of the most rascally character, and yet in the face of that you find the post office authorities of Canada, who I most emphatically state have the power to investigate this matter and bring the offenders to justice, failing to take any action. What have the post office authorities of the United States accomplished in the last few months in bringing to justice man after man in that country and not only exposing their methods but making them disgorge millions into the treasury of that country? Only last summer a man who was followed up by the postal authorities of the United States, greatly aided by the investigation of the editor of the Philadelphia ' North American,' was located in western Canada, brought back to the United States and forced to disgorge. Under the present government we have such loose management of the department as to allow this man, under the very eyes of the department, month after month, in spite of the articles that were appearing in the public press, to continue these illegal transactions all over this fair land of ours. Some of our papers have had the manliness and backbone to expose these different transactions, but I wish to say most emphatically that the time has come when the Dominion of Canada should appoint a public prosecutor, whose duty it will be to look into these transactions and who will have the power not only to investigate such transactions as those of Sheldon and the different loan' companies that have been exposed, but to examine, if necessary, the banks of this country in that respect.
Why did not the Solicitor General take up this matter? He knew full well that Sheldon was carrying on a most unfair and unbusinesslike proposition in the city of Montreal, and he is also open to censure. I am confining my remarks especially to the Post Office Department because that department, in answer to a question I placed on the Order Paper, simply said that all the responsibility they had or possibly could assume in regard to this matter was that they would notify the authorities of the province in which this man lived. It is well known that this man was conducting his business in Montreal, in the province of Quebec, but that he was also carrying it on in different provinces throughout Canada and especially in the province of Ontario. What power would the authorities in Ontario have to go to work and expose this man in the manner in which he should be exposed? The post office authorities say: Well, we did look into this matter two days before the man left-and they must have known months before that this man

had been carrying on his illegal transactions. Let me just call your attention to this fact that the department has no power, as they say, to institute prosecutions in such cases. This is not a sufficient reply where there is an implied charge of delinquencies. The question and answer have reference to a breach of section 209 of the Criminal Code:-[DOT]
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liaable to two years' imprisonment who posts for transmission or delivery by or through the post,-
(c} Any letter or circular concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive and defraud the public, or for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretenses.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: That is when he is found out.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that this is merely to be used when the guilty party is found out.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Is there anything under the Post Office Act which would authorize the Post Office Department to go into a broker's office to inquire into his transactions there?

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
That is a question from a lawyer which has nothing to do with the case. As far as I can see, it simply amounts to this that if the post office authorities knew for months, and I have no doubt that in their department they have had letters calling their attention to the transactions conducted by this man, and knew he was abusing the rights and privileges granted to him by this country under the Post Office Act, they are beyond any question very lax in the discharge of their duty towards the people of Canada. Referring to the British North America Act of 1867, I find that section 91 provides as follows:-
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the class of subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that, notwithstanding anything in this Act, the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated.
Let me call attention, to subsection 27:-
The criminal law, except the constitution of the courts of criminal jurisdiction, but including the procedure in criminal matters.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: That would all happen to Sheldon if he were brought before a jury.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Why is he not brought before a jury ? Is it not possible for the Minister of Justice to take action.? Is it not possible for the post office authorities to follow up men such as Sheldon, who have wrongfully taken money out of the mails ? Who is going to prosecute this man ?

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will bring Sheldon back, no doubt the government will take action.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
But why should the onus be put on me of bringing him back ? Why should the Minister of Justice shift his duty on to my shoulders ? Surely it cannot be pretended that it is not the duty of this government to set to work and have this man brought back to this country just as the United States government had men, under similar charges, brought back to their country. If it be said that the government have not the power to do this, it is time that they should take it. You cannot do any greater service to the people than expose just such transactions _ as Sheldon has been carrying on, and bring such men to punishment. Not only this man Sheldon, but his agents and satellites, his decoy men, who went around among the people, gathering in the dollars-these also, should be brought to justice. People were induced to part with their money on the representation that Sheldon would invest it for them, and return it to them with handsome profits. But what have we seen ? The auditor's report shows that Sheldon, instead of making by speculating, lost money, and what he did not lose in speculation, he took away with him. Thousands of people were thus defrauded out of their hard earned savings. The hon. gentleman knows full well that Sheldon sent off some $50,000 to Mexico, just a few days before leaving the country. Our ministers have in this, matter, become the laughing stock of the authorities of New York. Why ? Because they made the statement time and again, that if they had known about these things a few days after Sheldon left Canada, they could easily have arrested him. Every one apparently knew about him, except the government, and when the government did know, there was no one in it to take action. My hon. friend says:	Go on and take action yourself; go
on yourself, and hunt up this man. What an admission he there makes of _ the incompetency of this administration ! I submit that it is the duty of the government to take steps to put a stop to all these swindling and wild cat schemes. I hardly need tell you, Sir, that it is only a few years ago, since these Cobalt transactions were exposed, by which the people of Canada were robbed right and left, through reckless manipulation by men who had bogus companies to palm off upon the peo-

pie. Any number of these bogus mining propositions have been .shown up during the past few years. And no doubt, in the Porcupine district, you will find in the near future a number of similar companies foisted on our people. Since the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau), has referred to the Montreal Herald ' let me read him an advertisement which appeared in the Toronto ' Globe.' In that newspaper on October 8, the following appeared under a large display heading, and I want the Solicitor General to bear in mind this fact, that it was on the 11th of October Sheldon skipped .the country. Here is what appeared in the Toronto Globe on October 8:-[DOT]
C. D. Sheldon-Investor.
His plan of investment-Profits that have been made-Opportunity for investment.
Without sensational advertising, and without any unusual or extraordinary method, C. D. Sheldon, of Montreal, has created ? business involving an investment of over one million dollars a month for over 3,000 clients.
Mr. Sheldon s method's and successes have created such great interest throughout Canada that they have invited criticism, and natur-Mly excite both interest and curiosity.
The whole facts of Mr. Sheldon^s business are embodied in the following interview with the writer of this article:-
And I think it important this should be placed on record to show the position that even the newspapers have taken with re-ga.id to his trails action. In my opinion, the day is coming when newspapers will be made responsible for the advertisements they publish. I continue to quote from the advertisement. The ' Globe ' says to Mr. Sheldon:-*
Mr. Sheldon, you have made phenomenal profats for your clients during the past two years; can you give me an idea what these have amounted to?'
' The lowest profit made in any one month was 20 per cent, but the average has been between 30 per cent and 50 per cent. I made individual investments, but the increasing volume of business with the infinite detail made it necessary to change the system, so that the money now forms a common fund, and all investors receive the same percentage of profits.
Just imagine a prominent newspaper, which pretends to instruct the public, putting in an advertisement of this kind-a swindle on its face-offering to pay depositors profits of from 20 to 50 per cent per month and an average of 30 per cent per month. The interview continues as follows :-
' When you declare 20, 30 or 40 per cent a month if the profits are not taken out, do they become part of the principal, and begin earning with the original capital? '
' All profits not taken out are added to capital and immediately become active.'
' Mr. Sheldon, you are aware that you are accused of making extravagant promises. What promises do you make? What do you authorize your agents to make? '
' I make no promises, and the only authorization my agents have is to state facts as they are-to outline my plan of operation, and to say that I shall do all I can to produce results in the future as satisfactory as they have been in the past. I do not guarantee any fixed percentage of profit.'
' It has been suggested .that the only way in which such large profits can be paid is by applying later deposits to pay dividends on previous investments. What answer do you give this ' robbing Peter to pay Paul ' theory?'
' As I have during the past two years paid out in cash as profits over three times as much as I have received from my clients, this theory at once falls to the ground.'
' Do you guarantee against loss- '
'I do to the fullest possible extent. I protect all my investments, and never ask my clients to put up for margin, nor are my clients' investments ' wiped out ' by an unexpected decline in stocks.'
' What provision do you make for the inevitable but unexpected shrinkage? In declaring your monthly profits, do you create a reserve fund or are the total earnings allotted as profits- '
* Profits with safety ' is the central idea of my operations, so that I make ample provision to avoid being caught napping.'
That is only a portion of the advertisement. It merely goes to show that it is high time we had some public prosecutor who would prevent the publishing of such advertisements. It is not the man who is a plunger, and who is willing to throw from $200 to $500 on the chance of gaining, and not caring much if he loses. It does not matter to that man. But I have under my hand some of the most pitiful letters showing that these swindlers have gone to work, and, through their decoys, have made their alluring promises to poor widows and others in the towns and cities of Ontario in particular, and from these poor people have gathered up tens and hundreds of thousands of dollars to be squandered by these rascals, or taken to a foreign land. Language fails me to condemn a government that would allow such transactions to be carried on. If it be that this government has not power to follow this man, then a special duty rests upon this parliament to extend the government's power. This man ought to be followed even to-day. And that is why I ask the privilege of coming before the House at this time, for I believe that no time should be lost, but that this government should get to work, locate this man, bring him to justice and expose his methods as a warning to the people of Canada, so that, as far as possible, a recurrence of these swindles may be prevented. We know that, so far as Mr. Sheldon is concerned, he is a free man today, and the government, apparently, are taking no means to locate him.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: But they are.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) will tell us what they are doing.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Has not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) cited a section of the criminal law a moment ago under which Mr. Sheldon could be prosecuted? That is a question I ask the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) was going to answer a question. But if he is only going to ask questions that is a different matter. He has made a statement that the government, apparently, are taking action.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: With permission, I will answer that directly. The administration of the criminal law, from which the hon. gentleman has quoted, is in the hands of the provincial authorities, and the provincial authorities have taken action in this matter. There are warrants out and Sheldon is being followed.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
Then, it amounts to
this: The hon. gentleman distinctly admits that, so far as the Dominion government is concerned, they have taken no action.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: What action could the Dominion government take?

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) knows full well that the government of Canada are all-powerful. Why should we be compelled, as it were, to delegate to the provinces a matter of this kind? I have cited authorities to show that the Dominion government have the power to follow this man and bring him back to justice. If they have not that power, we should get to work and amend the British North America Act, so that the Dominion government may have power in such matters as these. Sheldon, as we are aware, operated in all the provinces. The government should investigate this case and give it all the publicity possible. I wish to say further that, not only have the officials of the province of Quebec, as far as I can learn, been negligent in this matter, but the officials of Montreal also are deserving of the severest censure.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: What about the Ontario government?

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
The statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) himself shows that the provincial authorities of Quebec have been notified in regard to this matter, and that it is within the powrer of the provincial government of Quebec to prosecute this man. But the hon. gentleman knows full well that the Ontario government has no powers over the mails of Canada. He knows, also, that the post office authorities Mr. ARMSTRONG.
have been most lax in this regard. I merely wish to emphasize this again by saying that the Dominion government should appoint a public prosecutor without further delay to investigate, not merely questions such as this coming before the Post Office Department, but similar questions coming before all departments of this government. There are questions in regard to election campaigns -that should be handled by this prosecutor. I cannot condemn too strongly the inaction of the government in this matter.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is on a similar footing to questions that I have raised in this House on former occasions. I contend that it is the duty of the federal authority to enforce federal law. And I am the more confirmed in that opinion because I find that, in some cases, we are doing it now. We enforce the Railway Act, we prosecute for infractions of the custom law and for crimes in connection with His Majesty's mails. There is a remarkable difference between the enforcement of federal law in Canada and the enforcement of federal law in the United States. In that country, when a federal law is passed, in order to protect the public, the law itself provides that it shall be the duty of the attorney general of the United States to enforce the law. And not only that, but every such law carries its own appropriation for its enforcement. This is true of the customs laws, the railway laws and the postal laws. The enforcement is not left to the state authorities. We read only last week of a case in which the post office inspectors of the United States raided a Wall street office, took the clerks, the typewriters and everything they could find, closed up the swindling concern and put the chief operators in jail. I contend on general grounds that if this parliament has power to make a law and does make a law, but does not enforce it, it is not doing its full duty, and is, in fact, an emasculated concern. I hope it will become more and more the rule, in accordance with what I have contended for in this House, that a federal law shall have provision for its own enforcement. For instance, we make election laws in this parliament in order to maintain purity of elections. If we do not ourselves enforce these laws we are not doing our duty. I commend to the attention of those concerned in this country the draughtsmanship of the federal laws of the United States, the directness and conciseness of expression. I commend to their attention, also, the wav in which these laws are enforced. The chief duty of the attorney general of the United States is the enforcement of the law. Furthermore, he is authorized to employ all kinds of legal as-

sistance and scientific experts, if necessary, to assist him. I remember being told in a similar case that I should go to the local authorities for enforcement of a law. I think that is altogether wrong, and that Acts made for the protection of the people should be enforced by the federal authorities, and in- cases of this kind by officers of the department. If anything wrong is being done in connection with the post office, the officers of that department should enforce the law, assisted by the attorney general of Canada.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Has the Postmaster General, or has he not, a right to intercept this man's mail, or any other mail sent by individuals in the form of posters, which, on the face of them, must be known to all intelligent people as of a fraudulent nature and likely to mislead the unwary, the result of which would be that they would be swindled out of their money? Has the Postmaster General the right to intercept such mail matter, and if so, were there reasonable grounds in this case for his taking action? Certainly he has the power to do so under the Post Office Act, if he thinks that a fraudulent business is being carried on by a firm or individuals. The hon. member for Lambton read an announcement that appeared in the ' Globe.' The interesting part of that to me is this: Was that put in the paper purposely as an advertisement for this firm? Now, if it appeared in a responsible and presumably respectable paper, without any adverse criticism, either in the editorial columns or otherwise, then I think in all fairness the paper ought to be held responsible for misleading the public, because no intelligent man on that staff, who read it, but must have known that the expectations of the individual set forth there could never be realized in the ordinary course of business, and it was his duty to prevent the public from being misled. If there is no adverse criticism in the paper, then I think the only conclusion that we can reach is that the paper is in league with the individual and helping him to swindle the public. I do not think, of course, that the government have anything to do with that, but I do not think it is very creditable to the newspaper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
I followed the remarks of my hon. friend from East Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) as closely as I could, and jf I understand him aright, he took occasion of the Sheldon case to bring again before the House a proposition which I think was brought up on another occasion, namely, that the. federal government should appoint a public prosecutor. This idea has been taken up also by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), who has brought it to the attention of the House
more than once. To-night the hon. gentleman, enlarging upon the idea, stated that in his opinion the federal government should look after infractions of federal law. A good deal might be said in favour of that view, and I am free to say to my hon. friend that had it been my privilege to have anything to do with the framing of the British North America Act, I certainly would have endeavoured to frame it in that direction. That is a provision in the American constitution, but unfortunately our constitution has not been so framed.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Does not the federal government provide a department to lay informations and to prosecute for breaches of the federal laws?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: My hon. friend from South York said that the federal government should look after infractions of federal law. I was going to say that in my opinion that would be a -proper policy. But I was also going to remark that in this respect the American constitution differed altogether from the Canadian constitution. The United States constitution has provided for federal courts to apply federal laws, and for state courts to apply state laws. Our constitution has provided only one class of courts, that is to say, provincial courts. All the laws of this country, whether enacted by the federal authority or by the provincial authorities, are administered by provincial courts.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: We have some federal courts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: We have no federal courts.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Yes, in regard to navigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: We have a court of admiralty.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: The Supreme Court has special jurisdiction, I think.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
The Supreme Court has special jurisdiction, it has also jurisdiction over provincial laws as well as federal laws. You can take an appeal from the provincial law in the province of Quebec that is an anomaly, and that anomaly has been enacted in our constitution. I do not think our system is the best one that could be devised, and I would have preferred if the fathers of confederation had followed the American system, and had established federal courts as well as provincial courts. But they have taken a different view, and we have only one system of courts, the provincial courts, which take cognizance of all laws, whether enacted by the federal or the provincial authorities. Therefore the view taken by my hon. friend is not logical. There is a good deal to be

said, however, in favour of having a public prosecutor, as they have in the United States, to look after offences against federal laws. I would be agreeable to that, but that is not in our constitution, and we have to apply the law as we have it.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: When a man violates the custom law, has not the Department of Customs power to fine him?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: There is nothing to prevent the federal government from enforcing its laws m the provincial courts, but we have only done so in rare instances. But my hon. friend who brought this matter before the House goes much further and he says it would be our duty to appoint a public prosecutor who should look after the enforcement of the Criminal Code. Now is there any reason for that? The only argument that he made for it was that Sheldon was at large. He argued as if Sheldon had not been prosecuted. But Sheldon has been prosecuted. There has been an information laid against him, a warrant has been issued against him, his case is before the courts of the province of Quebec. He has not yet been apprehended, but I understand that he is being followed, and that at any moment he may be found and extradition proceedings be taken against him. So if, in this instance, there had been a public prosecutor appointed by the federal government, it would not help the matter at all. The law in the province of Quebec has been in motion against Sheldon, a warrant has been issued against him. What more could the hon. gentleman desire? Whether that was done by the federal authority or by the provincial authority does not matter; the thing which the hon. gentleman wanted done has been done. Therefore, the hon. gentleman would be no further ahead than he is now, even if there had been in existence a public prosecutor appointed by the federal government. I think the hon. gentleman has been somewhat reckless in his statements. He has stated that in Cobalt and in the Porcupine district there is a notorious violation of the law.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
I am sure the right hon. gentleman does not wish to misinterpret my remarks. I would be very foolish to state that matters like this are being carried on in the Cobalt and Porcupine districts at the present time. What I meant was this:	I called attention to the fact
that a few years ago, in the Cobalt district, bogus companies weTe formed, plenty of them. The right hon. gentleman knows full well that in Gowganda there were lots of bogus companies formed and people were asked to subscribe two or three cents a share. The papers were full of all kinds of advertisements in connection with these matters. They were not investigated, these Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
men were not prosecuted and the same thing is true with respect to Porcupine. The Porcupine district is just being opened up and you can expect the same kind of manipulation there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: I suppose my hon. friend has brought this statement before the House in order to justify the conclusion that I should be a public prosecutor. That is what he had in view. Is there not a public prosecutor in the province of Ontario to-day? What is he doing? There is a public prosecutor to-day in Ontario. My hon. friend apparently is pot satisfied with the way the law is being administered in Ontario, and he says we should appoint a public prosecutor to do what the public prosecutor in Ontario fails to do?

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Would the public prosecutor have power to take up this Sheldon charge?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
There is a public prosecutor in Quebec, there is a public prosecutor in Ontario, but my hon. friend brought up this matter, about Gowganda, Porcupine and Cobalt, and he says that there were bogus companies organized, and that people were swindled out of hundreds of thousands of dollars. He brought this up in support of his argument that the time had come when the federal government should appoint a public prosecutor. Is there not a public prosecutor in Ontario? What is he doing? Does he allow people to be swindled out of hundreds of thousands? Does he want us to believe that he has no confidence in the government of Ontario ? I thought that Mr. Foy would have been sufficient for him. He pays us a great compliment-I do not object to it-but unfortunately we have been, up to the present time, depending upon the local government to do these very things. My hon. friend wants us to do that which should be done by the authorities of the province of Ontario. I have simply to tell him not to apply to us, but to go and ask his government, the government in which he has confidence, to do their duty as he thinks it ought to be done. But my hon. friend has also tried to read us a lesson which we do not deserve at all. The argument of my hon. friend has been based upon the charge that the postal authorities have failed to do their duty. If I understood him aright, he stated more; he stated that the postal authorities knew that Sheldon was filling the mails with illegal matter. That is a very strong statement, but my hon. friend has given no evidence to substantiate it. I do not think he can substantiate it, I do not think he can bring a tittle of evidence to show that the postal authorities knew what class of matter coming from the office of Sheldon

was going through the mails. If he has any evidence let him produce it, but I do not think he has any.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: May I ask the right hon. gentleman if the postal authorities had not received letters calling their attention to this matter, and if their attention was not called to the different papers that were exposing this fraud?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
I do not know whether it was or not; I take my information from the hon. gentleman. I am not the Postmaster General, I am acting in hi's absence, but I followed my hon. friend very closely, and if my hon. friend had any evidence that the post office authorities had received any such information I presume he would have brought it before the House. Therefore, I conclude from his silence that he had no such evidence before him, because he would not have been slow to have placed it before the House if he had known of it. The Postmaster General, as far as I know, had no such information. It is true that there were advertisements in the newspapers, posters and things of that kind. My hon. friend spoke of these, but he did not say that any evidence was placed before the post office authorities. But, if such evidence had come before the post office authorities what could they have done? The only thing they could have done was to have acted according to the law. The law does not give the department power to take any action. The only thing it can do, the moment any such information is brought to its attention, is to refuse the privilege of the mails to the parties who are guilty of such an offence. The law does not go any further, the law may be insufficient in that respect, it may be that my hon. friend is of the opinion that it should go further and that we should put in the law a provision which would give more power to the Postmaster General. But, at the present time the moment the Postmaster General has a suspicion-not only information, but a suspicion-or reason to believe that the matter posted is of an illegal character, he can close the mails to the parties so using them. I will quote to my hon. friend upon this point both the law and the regulations. Section 9 of the Post Office Act is as follows:
The Postmaster General may, subject to the provisions of this Act make regulations declaring what shall and what shall not be deemed to be mailable matter for the purposes of this Act, and for restricting within reasonable limits the weight and dimensions of letters and packets and other articles sent by post.
And so on. So, he can make regulations and the regulations are to be found in the book which is in the hands of every hon.
member. I quote from official postal guide, section 196:
If it be established to the satisfaction of the Postmaster General that any person is engaged or represents himself as engaged in the business of publishing any obscene or immoral books, pamphlets, pictures, prints, engravings, lithographs, photographs or other publications-or in the business of an illegal lottery, so called gift concerts, or other similar enterprise offering prizes or concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive or defraud the public for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretenses or in the business of selling or in any wise disposing of counterfeit money, or what is commonly called 'green goods,' or of drugs, medicines,-
And so on.
-and if such person shall in the opinion of the Postmaster General endeavour to use the post office for the promotion of such business, or if it be established to the satisfaction of the Postmaster General that any persons are using, or endeavouring to use the post office for any fraudulent purpose, then, in any such case it is hereby declared that no letter, packet, parcel, newspaper, book or other thing sent or sought to be sent through the post office by or on behalf of or to or on behalf of such person shall be deemed mailable matter.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Is there no provision by which a person may be punished for using the mails for any such purpose ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: No, there is not. The only thing is, that the Postmaster General, if he has reason to believe that an illegal business of this kind is being carried on, generally notifies the Attorney General of the province to take such action as is deemed proper.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Surely under the Code there is authority to take action against a party under these circumstances ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Certainly, under the Code, but the Code is not within the power of the Postmaster General. The Code is to be applied by the provincial authorities. I would like to say to my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) that the career, of Sheldon in this country, has been rather short and spectacular. He came in and carried on for some time, a very doubtful business. There were people who believed what he said, and they were made victims, but he was found out, when found out he had to leave the country, and he cannot come back again, because he would render himself liable to prosecution. I do not think that the post office authorities are in any way to blame in regard to the question which the hon. gentleman has brought before the House.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
I say it is possible, under the British North America



Act, to arrange for the enforcement of the Federal Law. The statement that the department has no power to institute proceedings, is a stupid statement; it is not true, either in fact or in law. The department, or the officials of the department have ithe same power to institute proceedings as any other individual. The institution of criminal proceedings is the laying of an information, and this has been shown to be an indictable offence, under section '209 subsection (c) of the Criminal Code:-
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who posts for transmission or delivery by or through the post,

(c) any letter or circular concerning schemes devised or intended to deceive and defraud the public, or for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretenses.
Then following this up a little further, section 654 of the Criminal Code directs us as to the institution of criminal proceedings :-
Any one who, upon reasonable or probable grounds, believes that any person has committed an indictable offence under this Act may make a complaint or lay an information in writing and under oath before any magistrate or justice having jurisdiction to issue a warrant or summons against such accused person in respect of such offence.
The following sections go on to state that after inquiry the magistrate or justice shall issue his summons or warrant. Therefore, there was nothing to prevent the officials of the post office taking proceedings, and it was their duty when they became aware of Mr. MACLEAN (York.)

There is another matter with regard to which I would like to say one word. I have followed very carefully the reading, by the Prime Minister, of the provision of the law which enables the Postmaster General to make regulations, and likewise the regulations which the Postmaster General made, and if I grasp it correctly, it is there specially provided that if the Postmaster General has reason to believe that any one is using the mails for swindling purposes, the Postmaster General may close; the mails to letters going to that swindler as well as to letters coming from him.. Are we to understand that the conferring of that power upon the Postmaster General imposes no duty on him? When it is a matter of public notoriety that a particular individual is spreading broadcast over this country through the mails, that he is prepared to receive people's money and earn for them as much as 50 per cent per month, are we to assume that the' Postmaster General is the only man in the country who has not the knowledge of these swindling operations. Sheldon was at particular pains to make known to everybody his pretensions, and' if not the Postmaster General personally certainly his representatives in the city of Montreal must have had knowledge of the transactions which Sheldon himself was at no pains to hide. Is the Postmaster General and is the government doing its duty now when they sit back and say: Oh. Sheldon has got away with the hundreds of thousands of dollars which he accumulated by means of letters circulated broadcast through the mails of Canada, we had no reason to suspect that he was carrying on his swindling operations through the mails and we have no responsibility in the matter. I believe that every man of fair common sense realized, when he saw these announcements of Sheldon, that there

must be a swindle at the bottom of it, and yet, this government, or the Postmaster General, who alone had power to protech the people, allowed his operations to be carried on, and now claim that it is for the provincial officers to look after Sheldon. I think the people will hold that the department of the Postmaster General is censurable for allowing Sheldon to continue his operations uninterruptedly for such a length of time.

To charge the Post Office Department with being negligent in their duty, you must show that Sheldon has used the mails to defraud the people by sending through the mails some articles that come under the Criminal Code. I am satisfied that if I were to spend thousands and thousands of dollars in advertisements, as was done by Sheldon, I would not take the trouble to print a little circular that would be seen by no one and would probably be put in the waste basket, ana send it through the mail. The Prime Minister has said that he thought the member for East Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) has brought the question up for the purpose of raising again the question of appointing a public prosecutor. To show the animus, I may say that tne first campaign in Montreal against Sheldon was opened by the Montreal ' Herald,' and the first challenge to Sheldon to show up his books, and the first challenge accepted by any paper to put up $500 or $1,000 was by the Montreal ' Herald.' Needless to say every one has discovered before this that the ' Herald ' is a Grit paper. maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
Having been at one time Postmaster General, I thought that I had some knowledge of the rules and regulations governing that important department. My hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau) avoids the question altogether. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister has tried to explain it. The charge made by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is that a series of frauds were being perpetrated through the mails with the knowledge of the whole community, and neither the Solicitor General nor the Post Office Department took any cognizance of them. The right hon. the Prime Minister says we have no jurisdiction, that our constitutional authority differs from that of the United States, and that, under the federal system in the United States, there is an attorney general and a fund for such prosecutions, which we have not. Well, we know that the United States government are very careful to prevent the use of the mails for improper purposes and to punish those who so use them. Here, it is argued, that the enforcement of the law is in the hands of our provincial authorities, and this government has no jurisdiction. Sir, the enforcement of the law and

the initiation of proceedings lie with this government. Where the mails are being used for fraudulent purposes the Post Office Department should institute proceedings. That department should lay the information. Has it done anything in this matter? It was to the knowledge of every man in the community at large that our people were being swindled and that our mails were being used to promote this swindling, and nothing whatever was done. The onus of taking proceedings was left to private individuals or the provincial [DOT]authorities. That is simply a farce. When our postal system is being used in any way for the purposes of crime it is for our Post Office Department itself to institute proceedings. Information, if necessary, is obtained, and the Solicitor General or the Minister of Justice, or the Postmaster General takes proceedings. The provincial authorities mav be used for the purpose of carrying out the law, but that is only a form of proceeding, the initiative rests with this government. I at first thought that the Solicitor General was giving the House to understand that he had done something, but when I listened carefully to him I found that the only thing done was the issue of a warrant at the instance of the attorney general of the province of Quebec -and a warrant, not for any crime committed against the Code, not for anything against the regulations of the Post Office Department at all. No, but for a crime against citizens of the province of Quebec -either theft or something else analogous, for swindling, but for the crime of utilizing His Majesty's mails, no action was taken. Whoever is at the head of the Post Office Department is responsible to see that nothing goes through the mails for the purpose of swindling. When any of these wrongs is committed it is the duty of the Post Office Department to initiate proceedings and bring the parties to punishment. And the responsibility of taking action rests upon the department; there is no reason to throw upon private parties the duty of calling the attention of these officers to these notorious crimes. Every one in the community knew that a crime was being perpetrated, and it was the duty of the government to prevent it.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Haggart) will allow me a question. He goes on the assumption that the mails were being used by Sheldon for this purpose. Is there any evidence of that before the House other than that produced by the hon. member for East Lambton?
