speechtext:
It was notorious that the mails were being thus used. I drew my information from what I saw in the newspapers, and from the statement of mv hon. friend from East Mr. HAGGART (Lanark.)
Lambton and others that circulars were issued to all parts of the country with statements that could not be other than fraudulent. And as a result of these circulars and of letters sent through the mails, people are induced to make investments of this kind.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: This case as it was presented to the House by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) is certainly a serious one, but I am bound to say that its seriousness, from the public standpoint, is greatly added to by the extraordinary position, as it appears to me, taken by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the still more extraordinary position taken by the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau). It is quite manifest that the mails of this country were used contrary to a section of the Criminal Code which I need not read to the House again. That section clearly made a crime of that which was done. The position of the Prime Minister, apparently-and I hops if I am wrong he will correct me, for the public should not be left in doubt on this understanding on this question-is that, in case of crimes against the post office, the railways and canals, the marine and fisheries, the interior or any other public service of this country, no prosecution is to be made unless some ordinary individual will apply to the provincial authorities. And when he applies, what is he to say? Why, that crimes are being committed against the property of the Dominion of Canada, against the administration of affairs.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Nobody ever said that.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) can speak if he wishes to. I am stating what seems to me the necessary inference from what was stated by the Prime Minister and by himself.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
Oh, yes. The Prime Minister asked why my hon. friend from East Lambton did not go to the Attorney General of the .province of Ontario and complain. Complain about what? About the use of the mails contrary to the regulations of the department and the Criminal Code. And yet both the mails and the Criminal law are matters under Dominion jurisdiction. If a registered letter is stolen in the city of St. Catharines, for instance, who prosecutes the thief? Does somebody who happens to hear of it prosecute the man? Does the man who sent the letter prosecute? No ; the post office inspector comes and lays the information. When a portion of the Welland canal was blown up with dynamite a few years ago, who prosecuted the criminals? Did this government leave it to the Attorney Gen-

eral of Ontario-the office then being occupied by a political friend of their own? Who prosecuted these men and had them sent to penitentiary for life for this heinous offence against the property of the King represented by the Dominion government? If on the Intercolonial a train were wrecked by gross criminal action, would this government have us understand that the Attorney 'General of the province in which the wreck took place would be left to prosecute the criminal? Yet, that would be the logical result of what the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General say. A crime is committed, but these gentlemen say they do not know that they can prove it. How are they to begin to prove it until they arrest the man? The Prime Minister and the Solicitor General say, in effect, that they can do nothing until the man is arrested. But how is the man to be arrested? Would these hon. gentlemen wait until the man comes in at their door and says : ' I have committed an offence against this country and I have come here to make sure that you shall not be embarrassed in prosecuting me? ' When a crime has been committed, somebody lays an information. And who ought to lay it if not the officer whose business it is to prevent infraction of the law? Why, the answer of the government in this case is no answer at all, because they are saying they cannot do in this case what it is quite common for them to do in many similar cases. Talk about subterfuges ; talk about special reasons for bringing matters before this House-if the Solicitor General wishes to talk in that way, I think he should talk into the looking-glass. If the Solicitor General has any duties-and you would think from the way he talks here that he had not, for he said it was not his duty to do this and not his duty to do that-it would seem that his principal duty is to find fault with those who wish to have this government do its duty in the enforcing of the law. Is swindling to be carried on through the mails controlled by the Dominion government because the provincial government, which has nothing to do with the mails, does not prevent it? If a citizen went to Mr. Foy, the Attorney General of Ontario, and asked him to prosecute this man, Mr. Foy would tell him that some one must lay an information. And who is to lay that information? If the officers of the Post Office Department do not lay that information, would not that fact make the man who laid it more or less liable to action for malicious prosecuton, he having acted when he was not called upon by any official duty?

My hon. friend will take note that the language of the advertisements is untrue. The Solicitor General says that they deceived intelligent people. If' they deceived only half-witted people they would not be half so fraudulent as they were in deceiving intelligent people like the hon. gentleman who has just asked me the question, and like the Solicitor General. But they were so fraudulent, so absolutely condemnable, so tricky and well conceived in their iniquity that they deceived all the generous minded, liberal minded and intelligent members of the Do-

minion cabinet, including the Solicitor General, and they caused a lot of people to be swindled. I do not speculate myself I have no money to do it with; and besides I think it is stupid; I do not know if any one in this House did in this case. But it is notorious, and was notorious at the time, that the Solicitor General got his political friends in the province of Quebec to do something. I am saying that when it is a federal matter the Solicitor General ought to have attended to it himself; and he had no right to ask the provincial authorities of Quebec, who might or might not be looking at it in the same way as he did, to prosecute in a federal matter, and- to get out of all responsibility in the House here by saying that he did something, and I suppose he meant the Dominion government, or the department. But it turned out -afterwards that the Dominion government did nothing, but that their political friends in Quebec did do something. That is to say, after the horse had been stolen, they went and locked the door so that the horse could not come back and get in again; that is all. But these mails were being used, they were being used improperly, it turns out that they had been used improperly for a long time, and there came a time when my hon. friend's own political friends in the province of Quebec, according to his own statement, saw that they were being used improperly, and they attempted to arrest the man after he had left the country.
But I am pointing out here that this is not the defence the Prime Minister put up in answer to the hon. member for East Lambton. The Prime Minister endeavoured to lay down the principle that in any case it was the duty of the provincial authorities to prosecute. He gave us to understand that, unfortunately, our system was not as good a system as they have to the south of us, he thinks that, unfortunately, we are trammelled, we are more or less tied up and shackled by the want of a new constitution, in order, forsooth, that a Postmaster General may arrest somebody who interferes with the mails. Now, what is meant by prosecuting a man? It is not done by the authority in the province of Quebec which appoints a crown attorney or crown counsel, who acts under a jury system. The gist of a prosecution is that some one shall lay an information and cause the man to be arrested and put upon his trial, who shall take the responsibility of seeing that that man is thoroughly tried, and if found guilty is punished, and who shall also become responsible for all the expenses connected with the prosecution? Was that done in this case? Not one iota of an attempt was made by any department of the Dominion government to do anything of the kind, and no apology is offered by the Prime Minister, who says Mr. LANCASTER.	j
practically to the people of this country: That is all you can expect from us, as long as we hold the reins of power, in regard to frauds and crimes against Dominion laws. Now, my hon. friend the Solicitor General made one or two references in which I do not think the Canadian people will agree with him. They had no power, he said, except to refuse the mails; the Prime Minister said so too. They make regulations, but they have no power except to refuse the mails to these people. Now. they have the power to investigate to see whether a crime has been committed.

In a criminal case, it is not the individual wronged, who has the right to prosecute. The crime is committed against the whole nation. If my hon. friend is wronged, if he is cheated, if his money has been stolen from him, the crime under British law, is not against him alone, it is against the whole nation, it is against the government who are the trustees of the people, and who are supposed to protect -the public at large against such crimes. Now the Solicitor General said he had a good deal of sympathy for these poor victims, they were* intelligent people, but that the thing was done, and -he had to get his man first. He had a good deal of sympathy for these poor victims, Mr. Speaker, sympathy from -a Solicitor General is not what the people are expecting, it is not what he is supposed to give. He -is expected to apply the law, pursuant to his title as Solicitor General. We can all have sympathy, without being Solicitors General or prosecuting attorneys. What is expected from the Solicitor General is not sympathy, but it is some action against the criminal.

Let me put this to the Solicitor General, if he does not know how the inference is irresistible. If somebody pointed a pistol at his head, ten feet away from him, and shot him, no one would see the bullet hit him. But because the man drew the trigger, and because the bullet was found in the hon. gentleman's head, the inference is, that he was shot by the man who pulled that trigger. When somebody is hit by somebody else and dies as a result, a jury will easily recognize the criminal. But in this case, the Solicitor General says there is no evidence. Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring, subject to various interruptions about which I am not complaining at all for they all tend to let tne facts be more clearly elucidated, to point out what struck me as being the duty of the government in all such matters as these. As I was pointing out it is probably too late to do anything in this particular case. But, we ought to learn by experience, and if the government had, either through the Prime Minister or the Solicitor General, given us to understand-as I have found the government to do on more than one occasion during the last ten years in which my constituents have honoured me with a seat in this House-that they were sorry that this had happened and that they would take care that it does not happen again, we would have been inclined to say: Very well, mistakes will happen, even in the best regulated families, accidents will occur and misdeeds will take place. But, we had the Prime Minister, before six o'clock getting up and explaining that there was no reason why any complaint should be taken in this matter and practically saying that my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) who, in my humble opinion, has acted in the best interests of the people of this Dominion, was wasting the time of the
House in bringing this matter up. I know of no more important question than that of the general application of the doctrine which I was endeavouring to elucidate before six o'clock, if you can call it a doctrine or principle, or whatever the word may be which I, for want of sufficient ability, am not able to correctly express, or to find in the dictionary at this moment, to properly signify than that it is the duty of the government to prosecute people who make an improper use of the chances that may occur to them with regard to the various departments of the government. There can be no doubt but that an improper use was made of His Majesty's mails with regard to the wrong, the criminal action of this man Sheldon.
The Solicitor General does not know that there was any evidence upon which the man could be convicted. The Solicitor General did not try to find out whether there was any. I apprehend that with his ability, with his well known ingenuity, his great acumen in all these matters, without which I do not doubt for a minute that the Prime Minister would not honour him with the position which he holds as Solicitor General of this great country, the Solicitor General put forward the best defenee he could oh behalf of the government. It is notable, it is deplorable that in the whole defence which he put forward he did not pretend to say that he had made any investigation, that he had made any inquiry to ascertain whether there was any ground upon which to substantiate a case. But he _ apparently thinks that he was doing his " whole duty when he gave the country to understand that in so far as he knew, without any investigation having been made, without any proof having been presented to him, there was no reason for putting any one upon his trial. The hon. gentleman lives not far from the city of Montreal, he is able to understand and speak eloquently in both languages, he is able to understand the newspapers printed in both languages, and I have no doubt he reads the Montreal ' Daily Star.' Let me point out a date here which is significant. On the 11th October, and not until the 11th October, did this man Sheldon leave Montreal. Upon Monday the third day of October, eight days before he went away, within a distance of three hours travel by railway from this city, where the departments carry on their business, where the Solicitor General has his residence, where his office is, where the Postmaster General lives, and where the Post Office Department is administered, in the city of Montreal, this paper is published daily. On Monday the third of October it had this in large type so that it would attract attention, so that any body who could read at all could see it no matter if he were half blind:

Sheldon can make a wad of 512 millions.
If he takes $1,000,000 and makes 30 per cent a month for two years.
Flurry on Saturday owing to a rumour that proves to be correct.
A rumour which spread around the city on Saturday and caused quite a flurry among C. D. Sheldon's clients, was to the effect that Mr. Sheldon had been ' stung' as a result of the raid upon the Schaftels bucket shop in New York.' .
I might remark in passing that that was a bucket shop that was raided by the authorities in New York because of a bad, wicked, felonious and criminal use that they were making of their position in order to defraud the citizens of the neighbouring republic. I proceed to read:
One man at least, withdrew his account from the Sheldon office on the strength of it, but the ' Star ' learned to-day from a man who does business with Mr. Sheldon, that ho had no connection whatever with the Schaftels crowd. In fact, he stated that no broker in Montreal did business with Schaftels as the house had been in bad odour for some time, and a raid or collapse such as took place has been more or less anticipated.
Lots doing.
The end of the month is always a busy time around the Sheldon offices over the City and District Savings Bank, and there was plenty doing there Saturday.
One of Sheldon's clients who came out grasping a cheque for his profits stated that 25 per cent was the amount paid in September.
Judging from the tales Sheldon's agents, friends and boomers were telling about his scoop in power stock everybody was expecting a record month, but evidently the scooping power, like the circus, was not up to the advertisement.
Mr. Sheldon evidently does not do business with a bank as his cheques are drawrn on a St. James St. money exchange.
Millions to Burn.
Mr. Sheldon's agents claim he does $1,000,000 worth of business a month and pays an average of about 30 per cent a month.
Suppose he has $1,000,000, keeps it and adds SO per cent each month to the wad for two years.
The amount compounded reaches the pleasing total of $542,800,605.
Think of it; 542 millions.
It makes John D. Rockefeller look like a cripple in a poor house.
Next day Mr. Sheldon may light his furnace with million dollar cheques.
Did the Solicitor General ever read that? It is on the first page of the MontreaJ ' Daily Star ' of Monday October 3. Let me tell the Solicitor General that every day from this time until the 11th October, was before the horse ran away. This was before the unfortunate locking of the stable Mr. LANCASTER.
door took place. Did my hon. friend read that? If he did not he ought to have read it.
Think of it, 542 millions.
It makes John D. Rockefeller look like a cripple in a poor house.
Next year Mr. Sheldon may light his furnace with million dollar cheques.
Did the Solicitor General not suppose that some of the poor people of Canada were being swindled; did he suppose that money could be honestly made in that way? Had he investigated he would have obtained such letters as I have in my hand signed by this man Sheldon in Montreal and addressed to a man in Aylmer, Ontario. Part of the offence took place in Quebec and part in Ontario, and both provinces are under the jurisdiction of the Solicitor General, in criminal matters, but the attorney general of Ontario has no jurisdiction to prosecute in Quebec and the attorney general of Quebec has no jurisdiction in Ontario. We on this side of the House are not solicitors general but we recognize we have a duty to perform to the public, even though we have only the ordinary indemnity of members of parliament and not the special stipend that the Solicitor General gets as watch-dog of the people's rights. The Solicitor General is a sort of member of the cabinet; he might perhaps be more correctly described as a tyler at the door of the cabinet, partly in and partly out, but still getting $5,000 a year specially. If this debate accomplished nothing else it may draw from the government some declaration of the duties of the Solicitor General, and he himself having told us to-day that this was not his duty and that was not his duty and the other thing wras not his duty, if you take nothing from nothing you will still have nothing left for the Solicitor General to do. The members on this side of the House are not upon the government benches and they cannot censure post office officials who have neglected their duties, and they have not a force at their disposal to find out if the law has been infringed, but yet in this case they got plenty of evidence to stop this fraud in time if they had that power. I have here a letter written by Sheldon in Montreal to a man in Aylmer, Ontario.

Yes. It is dated July 16, 1910, and one paragraph of it* says:-
That party invested $600 in January, 1909. From that he has drawn more than $6,000 since and he still has several times his original investment.

Why, even an ordinary school boy, without being a solicitor general at all and/ without having the more than ordinary ability which is supposed to grace the holder of that office; why, even a school boy would _say on the basis of that statement, that Sheldon was a liar, that he was obtaining money under false pretenses for which he was liable to go to jail for fourteen years. If the Solicitor General put Sheldon on trial before a jury would he have any doubt that he would obtain a conviction? He may say that he did not know of that letter, but on October 3 the ' Star ' newspaper told him that this thing was going on, and from October 3 until Sheldon departed the ' Star ' newspaper kept at it and the Solicitor General could easily have proven that this man was committing fraud. Seriously, is not the Solicitor General ashamed of having said that only the attorney general of the province could deal with this matter? Sections 404 and 405 of the Criminal Code tell -what fraudulent purposes are, and section 209, subsection (e) says that what Sheldon did was a fraudulent purpose, and the Solicitor General knows full well that under these sections of the Code he would have an unanswerable case against Sheldon. If I were counsel for that man I could do nothing else but advise him to plead guilty and throw himself on the mercy of the court; oh, no, I would throw him on the mercy of the Solicitor General or the Prime Minister, because the court would say that the prisoner should not be allowed to escape punishment and the Solicitor General and the Prime Minister have allowed him to escape. The frauds. The frauds perpetrated by Sheldon were a direct infraction of the law with regard to the mails of this country, which are controlled by the Dominion authorities and with which the provincial authorities have nothing to do.
The Solicitor General asks how I know Sheldon used the mails for that purpose. Letters are not sent by airship or by telephone or by telegraph or by subterranean cable, they are sent through the mail-and if this is not a fraudulent use of the mail, I would like to know what the Solicitor General would consider a fraudulent use Had this been acted on this man would have been put upon his trial and would have been prosecuted by the Dominion government with all its resources, with its Dominion police and its force of detectives. If $25 was stolen from our office and I did not prosecute the thief, I would be quickly told I was derelict in my duty in not instituting proceedings and seeing that the offence was proved and the guilty person punished. If I failed to do so, I would not be setting a proper example to my family and to those employed in my office. But here the Solicitor General, who ought to
know these things are going on against the Post Office Department, says, not that he looked into it, and found that he could not succeed in the prosecution, but that the government of Ontario or Quebec should enter upon the prosecution. In this case, a man in Montreal, by using the mails, induced a man in Aylmer to send money to him by fraudulent representations contained in that letter. Part of the offence was committed in Montreal and part in Aylmer, in two different provinces. Who will say that this is a sufficient excuse for the government not prosecuting for the fraudulent use of the mails ? It has been said in the press that by his operations, Sheldon could have made Rockefeller look like a cripple in a poor house. The prosecution of such a man should be undertaken, not by an individual, but by some authority with great wealth and power, like the Dominion government. If some poor fellow committed a breach of the fishery law, or interfered with the Indians up north, he would De prosecuted by the Dominion government, and landed in prison. If he could prove that he would vote for the Laurier government, I do not, of course, know what would happen. I am not pretending to draw the inference that Sheldon is a Grit, but I would repeat the remark of a counsel in Hamilton, that he would not say that every Grit was one of this kind, but he never saw one of this kind who did not vote for the Grit party. It makes one think the Laurier government does not care much, and will not act in these cases, unless somebody, who is not concerned as much as they are, will come and lay the information and undertake the burden of prosecuting. I do not know what would happen after the man was prosecuted and convicted. I am reminded that Bill Miner escaped, nobody knows how, nobody tried very hard to find out. He got out, and the Dominion government does not hesitate to pass estimates to leave some poor fellow in jail in Kingston, who, under stress of excitement, might strike another, and be sentenced for two or three years, because he was not Sheldon and could not make Rockefeller look like a cripple in a poor house and he stays there. I have an instance in my own district. A young man of 18, went out for a holiday near Dunnville, he hired a horse, he spent his pocket money and was afraid to return the horse, because he had not enough to pay its hire for more than the one day. He kept it for three days, went around among some of his school fellows and foolishly took it home with him. He was sent down for two years. I wanted to get him home for Christmas, but I have not been able to do so. Of course, I am not finding fault with the judge who sent him to prison for horse-stealing, but I would like to know what you have to do to get the ear of the

Solicitor General or his deafness. There was a very significant deafness in the case of the Montreal ' Star.' That paper was not using a megaphone, but it was printing in large type what Sheldon was doing and had been publishing it for eight days before Sheldon went away, and if the Solicitor General had inquired at all, he would have found that Sheldon's course was the most fraudulent use of His Majesty's mails. The Postmaster General, I am told, was not in the country, but the Deputy Minister was, and there are many post office inspectors. If some young fellow purloins a registered letter or even an unregistered letter, who lays the information? Not the Hon. J. J. Foy, not the Whitney government, or any of their officials, or the officials of any province, but the Dominion post office inspector, who insists on the boy being punished. It must be clearly understood for all time, that although the provincial authorities control the courts in summoning juries, appointing sheriffs, selecting Crown counsel, &c., the Dominion government always, where it sees fit to do so, prosecutes and lays information in regard to crimes against the Dominion government, or against the machinery of any department operated by the Dominion government.
Why should not this man have been apprehended by the Dominion authorities? Who would find fault with them if they had apprehended him? Who would feel insulted or snubbed or hurt in his feelings because he was not allowed the esteemed privilege of prosecuting this man Sheldon who would make, as the Montreal ' Star ' said, John D. Rockefeller look like a cripple in a poor house? I never heard of any body who would find fault with the Dominion government for laying that information, or object one minute to their prosecuting this man. What will the good people of this Dominion think of our Prime Minister who tells us, as the right lion, gentleman did this afternoon, that this Dominion government has nothing whatever to do with prosecuting people and enforcing the law, but has only to do with the making of laws. Rob the post office and customs houses, blow up the Welland canal, blow up the Georgian Bay canal if it ever be built, put into the Newmarket canal, if you can find sufficient water to cover them, all the ballot boxes containing Conservative ballots-do anything you like, the Dominion government will not prosecute. If you are to be prosecuted, that must be done by the provincial attorney general. That is the slogan, I suppose, for the next elections. Deal in every malicious, criminal, improper practice you can think of, you need have no fear of the Dominion government. Only stand in with the attorney general of the Dominion, and you will never be prosecuted. If I have Mr. LANCASTER.
drawn a wrong inference-and I know the Solicitor General does not like inferences, because he told us so this afternoon-I am very sorry, but human nature is such that I am bound to use what little common sense I am blessed with and my limited intelligence

speechtext: Those who are laughing, laugh because they have not sufficient intelligence to do anything else. There is a certain animal that can laugh and do nothing else; there is a certain other animal that can bray and do nothing else; and judging from the arguments we had from them this afternoon, there is a menagerie on that side of the House. Before proceeding further, I should like to emphasize again the point I am endeavouring to make. The affairs of the country require to be carried on with something else than laughs and brays. When we have to listen to the arguments that the Dominion government is powerless to enforce its own laws, but has to leave their enforcement to the discretion of the attorneys general of the provinces, or to private individuals, then we can only conclude that every member of parliamenttaking the argument of the Solicitor General-will have to take up that hon. gentleman's duties and do for this overworked and highly paid attache of the cabinet, what he is helpless to do himself.

maintopic: ILLEGAL USE OF MAILS-CASE OF C.
speechtext:
As I listened to the reply made by the hon. the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau) to the very serious charges brought against his administration, my thoughts were carried back to the days when I listened to comic opera, and when one particular ditty impressed itself very cogently upon my youthful imagination and musical propensities.
When constabulary duty's to be done,
A policeman's lot is not a happy one.
Those lines very happily hit off the condition of the Solicitor General. When there is question of policing the rights and wrongs of the people of Canada, his lot, and that of his government, is anything but a happy one. When the people of Canada are outraged, when their money is stolen by devices so barefaced that only the helpless could be taken in by them, we have our Solicitor General, speaking for the Department of Justice, declaring that in order to get redress we must go to the attorney general of Ontario, and not to this government. Although our laws prohibit the use of the mails by any one for improper purposes, yet our Solicitor General tells us that this government is absolutely helpless to enforce that law, that its hand is paralysed, and that, no matter 1 what may be the infractions of that law.

our Justice Department can do nothing and we must seek a remedy at the hands of the provincial government. The hon. the Solicitor General tried to fasten all the responsibility upon the attorney general of the province of Ontario. How great is that responsibility, especially when that attorney general happens to be a Conservative. Were he a Liberal, his responsibilities would not be nearly so great. But such was not always the case. There is a reverse side. As the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) said: You ask them to sing ' Rule Britannia and they sing ' Kathleen Mavourneen ' because it creates more ' divarsion '. Let me remind the right hon. the Prime Minister and I shall not go back 20 years or 10 years or even one year.
I "will go back only six months. I want to talk to that right hon. gentleman face to face about the facts that have been brought out in this House and that are on our records. What happened with regard to the prosecution of Messrs. King and Skill in Toronto for the use of the mails for obscene and filthy literature? Was the advice of the Solicitor General taken there? Yes, taken to the full. The government went to the attorney general of Ontario. The Post Office Department complained, the Gustoms Department complained, that Messrs. King and Skill were using His Majesty's mails for the purpose of conveying obscene and filthy literature contrary to the Criminal Code and to the postal and customs laws. The attorney general of Ontario promptly prosecuted, Messrs. King and Skill, after several adjournments, pleaded guilty. Then the matter came before the Justice Department represented by the Solicitor General. And, notwithstanding that the Post Office Department had prosecuted, notwithstanding that the Customs Department had complained, notwithstanding that independent investigation had shown that the literature complained of was filthy and obscene, notwithstanding that the men had pleaded guilty, my hon. friends' (Mr. Bureau's) department pardoned these men and freed them from custody. Mr. Speaker, that is what we get for taking the dictum of the Solicitor General and going to the attorney general of Ontario, so long as the Solicitor General, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister have their hands on the controlling lever, the pardoning power. Yet the Solicitor General comes here to-day and tells us to repeat this. Do the same thing with Sheldon, he says, and we will repeat the trick. These men were Liberals, and they were got out by the recommendation of Liberal politicians, men holding Liberal positions in Liberal organizations. And the literature was put right under the nose of the Prime Minister by a deputation of clergymen, and I defy the right hon. gentleman
to say that that literature was not filthy and obscene. This sort of thing has been going on from time to time. And I say that great credit is due to the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), who has brought this to the attention of the government and to the hon. gentlemen who have supported him. This is not a case that is to be laughed out of court. But I say with all due respect to the office of the Solicitor General that, in my opinion, that hon. gentleman did not treat this matter with the gravity it deserved. I do not think he treated the legal aspect of it with the depth and wisdom that one would expect from a gentleman occupying his position. On the contrary, he was rather facetious on the whole subject, and seemed inclined to resort to the very questionable method of laughing it out of court. It is a very pitiful exhibition of weakness if this government, from the Prime Minister down, is to take the position that there is a law on the statute-book of Canada which this government is incapable of enforcing as against offenders. Under the rule laid down, I can rob the mails, I can make use of the mails to disseminate filthy and obscene literature, such as has been put under the nose of the Prime Minister himself, I can import that literature through the mails, in defiance of the customs law and the postal law, with absolutely no result, because the Justice Department of this government will pardon the offender if he be of the right political stripe. That sort of thing cannot continue; the people of Canada will not tolerate it. The people of Canada expect the government to be in a position to enforce its laws and that it shall have the vigilance and the moral force, when it sees an infraction of the law, to bring the criminals to justice.
We hear a great deal about locking the stable door after the horse has been stolen, as exemplified year after year bv the actions of this government. Three or four sessions ago we had a very clear instance of it in the Department of the Interior. A great deal of timber had been disposed of by the Department of the Interior in a very questionable way. But after that a drastic policy was laid down by the department- locking the stable door of our timber lands after the horse was gone. Another instance -do we remember it, or-or have we short memories? Do we remember how the Prime Minister stated from his place in this House that the Marine and Fisheries Department had run riot-that it was so extravagant that it had 'run riot '? Do we remember what the investigation into that department disclosed? Do we remember how the middleman flourished? Do we remember how Merwin flourished? And how hundreds of thousands of dollars were stolen from that department by middlemen?

But there came a day when it was found that the horse was gone. The people of Canada had found it out, and they would stand that kind of thing no longer. Then, with righteous indignation that such a thing could happen, this government locked the stable doors of the Marine Department. And it was stated-with a very merry wink behind the hand-that the middleman was known no more, that the patronage list had been abolished, that, forever and a day the stable door of the Marine Department was locked fast. Recently we had another very cogent instance. And I am sorry that the Secretary of State (Mr. Murphy) is not in his place. This side of the House has called attention, session after session, to irregularities in the Printing Department. There was an investigation during recess, and a wonderful demonstration of the power of our Secretary of State-and the stable door of the Printing Department has apparently been closed. And so with other departments in which investigations have been made and in which demonstrations of weakness and dishonesty have been made. I say this is a case of no small importance to the people of Canada. If the people of Canada are liable to be preyed upon by such men as Sheldon, if His Majesty's mails are to continue to be used for the purpose of disseminating literature Containing representations intended to induce people to invest their hard-earned savings in fraudulent schemes we have the most striking evidence of the weakness, the absolute incapacity of the government when it says that it can take no steps by which an offender of this kind can be deprived of the use of the mails and that clear evidence of the barefaced manner in which the thing is carried on is no evidence that can be taken by the Solicitor General. Sir, I think this is a matter that deserves more attention than has been given to it either by the Prime Minister or the Solicitor General, and the countrv owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. gentleman who has brought it to the attention of the House in so forcible a manner.

I should not rise to prolong the debate were it not for the misapprehension that exists in the House as to the reasons which deterred the Solicitor General from taking steps in this matter. In looking over the Auditor General's Report I have found the reason. As we know the facts, this man Sheldon had been using the Royal mails of Canada to send out absolutely false representations to the public, and to abstract dishonestly from the people their hard earned money. It was a notorious get-rich-quick scheme, and was successful to an extent which we all deplore. There was no contention by the Solicitor General that this scheme of Sheldon was anything else than an absolute fraud, a Mr. BOYCE.
gross steal. We have had from hon. gentlemen on this side of the House various suggestions as to why the government, who were elected to protect the people from frauds of this kind, did not do their duty. I have found out the reason, and I am going to give it to you, Mr. Speaker. On page 90-V of the Auditor General's Report of this year, on the fifth line, we read: * Solicitor's General's Office,' $41.40. Small payments and desk, $32.40 ; 2 clocks, repair, $5.' I gather from the care which the Solicitor General has shown for the people of Canada that he found it necessary to have two alarm clocks to keep him awake to the situation. In that case, I fancy, if the alarm clocks were working as they should have worked he might have been awake. But the next item shows that they were not working properly, for we find an item of $5 charged to the people of Canada for repairing these clocks. In addition to that, the hon. gentleman had to buy a pillow, at $4. Now when you see such an account as that for a pillow on which the hon. gentleman could sleep in working hours, there is no longer any reason why any hon. member on this side should find fault with him for neglecting his duties. I think, Mr. Speaker, by the way you are nodding, that you agree with me.

speechtext:
I am surprised that the government have not taken more interest in this question than they appear to have done. The Prime Minister has placed all the responsibility on the provincial governments, and the Solicitor General takes the position that they have no responsibility at all, that this government is in no way responsible for the rascally work that has been carried on in this country for the last two years. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot find language strong enough in which to condemn the government for their inactivity in regard to this whole transaction, when you find this man Sheldon had been carrying on his nefarious work month after month, without any hindrance. The Solicitor General talks about the Montreal 'Herald,' and says: Why don't you give the Montreal 'Herald' credit for its splendid work in exposing this man's fraud? Well, Sir, if the Solicitor General read the Montreal 'Herald,' why did he not take some action in the matter? If he believed the words of the Montreal 'Herald,' his own organ, why didn't he go to work and investigate these transactions and prosecute this man? Why did not the Postmaster General and some of his officers go to work and investigate this transaction? You will find in the pages of the 'Herald,' for some time previously, the strongest kind of condemnation. The Solicitor General asks why we do not quote from tne Montreal 'Herald!?' Well, I will quote from the Montreal 'Herald.' As I told the Solicitor General this afternoon, the Mon-

treal 'Herald,' while it pretended to expose the transaction, in the same breath was covering it up to a certain extent, and giving it free advertising. Let me call attention to what the 'Herald' said on October 4, in large headlines:-
Sheldon tired of making fortunes with others' money. . . . C. D. Sheldon, the investment broker who has startled the town, received a caller this morning in the person of a ' Herald ' representative and promised to answer many knotty points in his business methods in a letter to the ' Herald' in the next day or two.
Now, in the letter printed in this very paper what do we find? This letter says to the 'Herald' people:-
Mr. Sheldon is doing either a legitimate or an illegitimate business. If the latter, the ' Herald ' could very easily find out and with very little ado put him out of business; but if Sheldon is doing a perfectly legitimate business-which should be put a stop to-the man who takes you out of the lamb class or the one through whom you usually get counted in with it.
The Solicitor General knows that the 'Herald' could go to work and put a stop to the business, and so could the Solicitor General. I have just been handed the Toronto 'Globe' of this day, in which I find the following:-

Spencer, of 65 Sullivan street, 35 years old, had a scheme to make other people rich. The postal authorities, however, objected to the philanthrophy and Detective McKinney arrested the philanthropist on charge of using the mails for fraudulent purposes.
I would like to ask the Solicitor General how it is, if the postal authorities had power m this case to prosecute a man who had been defrauding the mails, they had not power to prosecute Sheldon, who had been defrauding the mails to an even greater extent. Why did not the postal authorities prosecute these men? Is it because there are prominent men among them who have influence with men on that side of the House to put a stop to these prosecutions being carried on? Let me call attention to this letter in the Montreal 'Herald' of October 4.
Yesterday Mr. Sheldon sent the following letter to the representative of the Crown prosecutor for the district of Montreal.
To the representatives of the Crown prosecutor for the district of Montreal:
Gentlemen,-In view of the recent attacks directed against my operations and more especially those which have appeared in certain local journals, and before the suggestion which has been made respecting an examination by the Crown prosecutor, I invite you cordially by this present, as representatives of the Crown prosecutor, to visit my offices at 180 St. James St., to examine all my hooks and accounts.	[DOT]
Doing this you will judge whether my business is legitimate, if the profits I have paid and am paying have been up to the present realized, and if my operations are conducted according to strictly honest business rules.
Yours very respectfully,
(Sgd.) C. D. Sheldon.
Why did not the district prosecutor of Montreal investigate these accounts? Was it not his duty to do so in face of the fact that day after day, paper after paper issued in Montreal was calling his attention to the circumstances? I would like to ask the Solicitor General if it is not a fact that the warrant was not issued for Sheldon's arrest until two days after he had left the country? Will the Solicitor General be good enough to answer that question?

He even allowed Mrs. Sheldon to leave Montreal and join Sheldon without being watched. After he left thousands of dollars came through the mails for him. They have not even begun to prosecute his agents, the decoy men, the middle men. They have become so accustomed to dealing with middlemen that they apparently cannot prosecute one of them. VERVILLE (Maisonneuve) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 3) respecting the hours of labour on public works. He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to go over the grounds that we traversed last year in connection with this Bill. It is pretty well known to members of this House what we did last year with regard to this proposition. A special committee was named last year which made an investigation, the report of which has been on the desk of every member here for a number of days, and in all probability the members have had an opportunity of reading the evidence which was given before that special committee. A great many people for and against this measure had an opportunity of presenting their views to the committee. The Bill which I have presented this year is very much the same as that which was before the House last year, but with some modification. In order to meet the views of a great many persons interested in this measure, I may say that I am willing to go a little further with respect to this Bill than I did last year. I want to introduce in this country, as they have in other parts of the world, a measure providing that the eight-hour principle shall be applied to a certain class of works. I am not so particular about the amount of work that it is applied to, provided we have on the statute-book, as they have in other countries, a measure of this kind. Having adopted the principle of this Act it may be that in a few years we will be in a position to extend it to other industries. I am willing this evening if we go into committee to present some amendments. I know that some Mr. MILLER,
hon. members are of opinion that the Bill is rather radical in some respects, and in so far as it respects individual concerns I would be willing to go even beyond the Bill that I have before the House at the present time. But of course I also consider the application of that measure, and consequently I am anxious that it should pass not only this House but the Senate and become the law of the land. maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The principle of this Bill is that eight hours shall constitute a day's work on public works in this country, and, representing an agricultural constituency, in Ontario, I desire to say that my constituents are diametrically opposed to that principle. A commission was issued by the government and much evidence was accumulated in respect to this Bill, and the sentiment of agriculturists throughout the country was strongly opposed to the principle contained in it. So far as I am personally concerned I wish to go on record as not only being against the individual sections of the Bill but against the whole principle of the Bill.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Last session when this matter came before the House, as representing an agricultural constituency I felt it my duty to enter my protest against the principle of an eight-hour day on government works. I repeat my objection now and I shall briefly give my reasons. One of the great problems confronting the agriculturists of the older provinces is the impossibility of getting adequate help on their farms, and from one end of Ontario to the other there are complaints along this line. It seems to me that no argument is necessary to prove that if you

make an eight-hour day on government works you are entering the thin end of the wedge, and that the eight-hour day principle will be followed with respect to all kinds of works. If men work for only eight hours a day on government works they certainly will not work for a greater number of hours on the farm. However, desirable it may be to shorten the hours of labour on the farm, every one who has been brought up among farmers knows well that an eight-hour day on the farm is entirely out of the question. This clause of the Bill sets out that it shall not apply to different kinds of work and there is a provision away down at the tail end of the section-and the agriculturists of Canada have always been at the tail end in the minds of this government whenever there is any legislation proposed [DOT] to improve the conditions of the people-at the tail end of the section there is a provision that it shall not apply to agricultural work, presumably because it is recognized that an eight-hour day is impossible on the farm. But, that does not relieve the situation, because if the day is eight hours on government work other industries will have to introduce the eight-hour system, and men will not work on the farm for 12 or 14 hours a day if they can make a living at other occupations by working eight hours. That is a question which should receive very careful consideration. There are I know many employments where an eight-hour day would be desirable ; for instance the case of miners working underground, but I protest against the principle in this Bill because it will undoubtedly work against the interests of the agricultural community. Besides that, I do not believe, judging of what I have seen of men working on government works, that they are overburdened with labour. Men on the farm who put in eight or ten hours at work, I venture to say do more real hard labour than men on government works would do in twice that time. I repeat that this is a matter that should receive very careful consideration because I believe it is a matter that is very strongly against the interests of the agricultural class.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Although this Bill has been before the House for some time, the promoter has told us that it is not the Bill in its present shape which he wishes us to consider, that it is his intention to propose several amendments; and the Minister of Labour has also told us that it is the Bill as the promoter wishes to amend it that will be considered. I think it only proper that we should have the Bill with his amendments before us before taking the matter up. I therefore beg to move that the committee rise.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I think the answer given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) to 45
the member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) is altogether unsatisfactory to this committee. My hon. friend has a department especially charged with the labour organizations and the labour questions of this country. My hon. friend has made that his life's work and his life's study; because of that he was taken into this government and he has had the question of whether or not it is right to adopt the principle of eight hours a day before him for many years. This question has been thrown this way and that way for many' years between the labour organizations of this country and the agricultural men until it is absolutely unsatisfactory to the people of Canada, and when we have an hon. gentleman occupying a position such as the Minister of Labour occupies it is only fair and just to this committee, when a Bill of this kind comes up for consideration, that my hon. friend should state frankly .and fairly whether he himself and the government that he supports are in favour of eight hours or not. I for one say that my hon. friend's answer was altogether too evasive at this stage of the discussion of this important question. There is not much distinction between my hon. friend and the gentleman behind him who is introducing the Bill (Mr. Verville). Every one knows that the Minister of Labour has consulted and discussed these proposed amendments. There has always been an understanding between these two gentlemen in the House and out of the House and this sparring between my hon. friends will not be accepted by this committee or by the people of Canada anyt longer. We have a right to expect, indeed I think I have a right to ask the right hon. gentleman to see to it, that this matter is not thrown from one side of the House to the other any longer. Either the government and the Minister of Labour are in favour of the principles of this Bill or they are opposed to it, and in fairness to the House and to this country, and particularly in fairness to the -hon. gentleman's friends, he has a right, I think, to state to this House frankly and fairly whether he is in favour of this Bill or opposed to it, so that we will not be having Bills of this kind introduced and withdrawn and referred to special committees from year to year and gentlemen running in constituencies upon this principle and that sort of thing any longer.
If my hon. friend has any work in his department at all, it seems to me that he could reach a conclusion in his own mind whether he is in favour of the 'principle of eight hours or not and if he has reached it he should state it frankly to this committee.

speechtext: If hon. members opposite will allow me to answer one question at a time, I will endeavour to do it. I have been asked first as to the Bill and then as to the principle of the Bill. I think the question as to whether or not I was infavour of the principle of an eight-hour-day was put in the first instance by the hon. member for Peel (Mr.- Blain). I do not wish to shirk an answer to that question at all. I would say frankly and freely that I am strongly in favour of the principle of an eight-hour-day, and the reason I am in favour of that principle is be-j cause of the belief which I have in the object of the existence of men on this earth. I think men are put here for some pui*pose other than that of simply spending their lives in toil, that every man should have an opportunity to work but that he should also have opportunity for a little leisure as well, that he should have an opportunity to spend part of his time with his wife and children whether he be a working man in a shop or a farmer, or an employee on a farm, or whoever he may be, that every man should have an opportunity of developing all the capacities with which he by nature may he endowed.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I shall answer any question the hon. member puts to me if he will allow me to finish what I am saying in answer to a question which he has already put to me. I was about to say, when I was interrupted, that if we stop to consider what the life of the average workingman is we will see how all-important it is that every one who has at heart the welfare of humanity should use what little influence he may have, whether in connection with the government or out of it* to help bring about a condition of affairs which in the course of time will secure to every man, whether working on a farm or in a workshop, a condition that will permit him to do eight hours' work and have part of the balance of the day for enjoyment and for the necessary development' of his faculties, one way or another.
Take the case of a workingman working 8 or 10 hours a day. Supposing he starts work at 7 o'clock in the morning, he must rise at 5, for workingmen have to start their own fires to assist their wives to prepare their breakfasts; five o'clock is as late as any man who is going to work at seven can afford to rise. He leaves his home before seven o'clock, having seen nothing of his children. He works from seven until 12, which is five hours. He goes back to his home, he has one hour in the middle of the day, part of which is lost going to and from his work. Sometimes he does not even get that. Sometimes he is obliged to take his dinner can and eat his cold meal at the workshop, and can see nothing of his home during that hour. Then he is obliged to work again from one to six o'clock; and if he is to have eight hours' sleep, which is the least he requires after a hard day's labour, that leaves him only from six to nine to enjoy the comforts of his home. It was never intended by the Creator that the great mass of men should live in that way. It was intended that every man should do his share of work and have opportunity to partake of legitimate enjoyment and develop the latent powers and talents with which he is endowed by nature. The working classes have as much

love for their families, as great regard for domestic happiness as the rich. They also require a little enjoyment now and then. The man on the farm wants the opportunity to go into the city occasionally, the labouring man wants his evenings the same as other people, and no one should be obliged to stay so long at work that he can have but three hours in the evening to appreciate his home and develop his aspirations towards a fuller life. Any other condition of society is not one which is fitting the prosperity we desire to see our country enjoy.
1 am strongly in favour of any movement which will help to bring about an eight-hour day, I recognize that such a day cannot be immediately of universal application. I recognize that in any one country you cannot bring that about without having regard to the conditions in other countries. This is an age of competition, not merely between industry and industry, locality and locality, but between country and country; and a country which enacts laws of a higher standard than another may find that in virtue of those very laws it may lose a whole industry simply because an adjoining country has not come up to that high standard. The men who have taken the keenest interest in this question realize that if the labour movement is to make headway, it can only do so by all countries uniting and agreeing to a similar standard. This year I had occasion to attend a meeting of the International Association for Labour Legislation at Lugano, Switzerland. That association was started in Berne in 1900 by men who recognized that if it were to be made possible to lessen the hours of working people, in particular to restrict the labour of women and children in any equitable manner that would have to be by agreement between such countries as France, Germany and England. All these countries should combine and mutually consent to maintain similar conditions. That association has done great work throughout Europe and the United States, and I hope that Canada will contribute its share to that work and help to bring about that uniformity of con ditions in different industries which will enable an employer, who would liae to reduce the hours of labour, to do so without running the risk of being undersold by less considerate rivals.
That brings me to another consideration, namely, the great difference in industries. In some the work is long and exacting, the toil exhausting, and there is a great nerve as well as physical strain which must be taken into account. In some cases, an eight-hour day would be altogether too long. I remember a few years ago investigating in Toronto conditions under which young women were operating the telephone 45i
exchanges. From testimony given by leading physicians, it was perfectly evident that no woman could continue in that kind of work and maintain her physical strength if she worked for a longer space of time at a spell than one hour and a half. She then reouired an intermission of rest before working another hour and a half, and a five-hour day was in her case sufficiently severe. While I am in favour of aiming at a given point, it may be that, in many occupations, an eight-hour day would be to long, and there may be others in which it would be too short. In many occupations seasonal conditions must be taken into account. In summer it may be' desirable to work longer than in winter. In some occupations the eight-hour day might to use an apparent contradiction-be a little longer or a little shorter than in others. But the great point to keep in mind is this, that unless some principle be laid down, we are not likely to arrive anywhere.
The question now suggests itself as to why the government should take an interest in this matter. Well, the supreme object of government should be to develop a happy and contented nation, and the only way to get a happy and a contented nation is to have the homes contented and happy. It is to the degree to which the artisan, the farmer, the great labouring classes are happy and prosperous that the nation is prosperous and contented. That condition you cannot have if our labouring men, working too long hours, are exhausted by toil and denied the opportunity of developing those qualities which make up a robust manhood. I have asked why the government should take an interest in this matter. There are many reasons. First of all, as I have said, it is the duty of the government to foster citizenship above everything .else, and you cannot have true citizenship unless you have men who are something more than mere machines, unless you have intelligent beings who know what is going on and have the capacity to take their share in the many sidedness of life. The government, recognizing that position, has to consider whether it has an opportunity to further this end. It so happens that the government is sometimes in the position of an ordinary employer cf labour. When it is, it should be a model employer; it should do what many an employer, if he were free to manage his own business as he would like, would seek to do. There is another consideration also which a government must keep in mind. A government is a trustee. It holds the funds of the people; and in dealing with industrial problems it has to take account of that fact as well. So that in this question of the eight-hour day, the government has to consider two things.

First of all, it should seek to be a model employer; and secondly it should bear in mind that it is a trustee holding the funds of the people; and, if I may add yet a third, it must have regard to industry in general, and seek, in its actions, to go just so far as it would be justified in going without undue interference with the ordinary course of business. To unduly interfere would be to retard the movement we are seeking to advance. There is a further point which should be kept in mind, particularly by the working people.
In this country, the power to legislate on labour matters is divided. There is the jurisdiction of the provinces and there is the jurisdiction of federal government. I have heard some members on the other side of this House say-they said it last session-that if the hon. member had introduced a Bill which would give an eight-hour day to everybody, they would support it. I do not wish to use the language I feel tempted to use in describing the attitude of one who would speak in that way. Every hon. member of this House knows that no Bill can be passed by the parliament of Canada which will give to the working classes generally an eight-hour day. They know that that is the business of the provinces primarily, _ that it is the duty of the provincial legislatures to fix the hours of labour governing any particular industries. One of the greatest services ever rendered to the people of this country was rendered by the hon. member who introduced this Bill when he succeeded in getting the Bill referred to a special committee and brought before that * committee the mass of evidence contained in the committee's report. Hon. members who have read that report will see that from the testimony given by different classes, there is the strongest reason why this government should set an example, and why the provincial governments should seek to do more than they have been doing in the way of studying the condition of men, and more particularly of women and children, employed in industries. This volume of evidence is one of the best contributions ever made to the question of the eight-hour day. That committee held, altogether, I think, nineteen meetings. It obtained representations from the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, from the Canadian Manufacturers Association, from the Shipping Federation, from large numbers of employers, from the factory inspectors, from officers ot the provincial government, from large delegations of different classes of the community including the Dominion grange, the farmers' institutes, the breeders' associations, the marine interests, the trades and labour unions, the transportation companies and others who felt that the measure introduced might Mr. KING.
affect their interests. What was the result of that evidence? It is to be found in part in the Bill which the hon. member (Mr. Verville) has brought down. And, if he has left agriculture out of that Bill, it is because the evidence given before that committee last year was that a law fixing an eight-hour day would not, as respects agriculture, be favoured by agriculturists and would not be in their interest. The hon. gentleman has considered the testimony given by all classes and he has endeavoured to bring down a Bill which is along lines that take into account the representations made by the farmers and those on their behalf, by the manufacturers and those on their behalf, as well as the interests which were represented by the labour councils. So, I think this House can afford to consider carefully the measure which the hon. member for Maisonneuve has introduced. And it will only be doing what the people of this country expect it to do if it makes a beginning by asserting the principle that the government of the country should be a model employer of labour. The one consideration that has to be kept in mind is this-that you can begin a reform in two ways. You can start with the broad end of the wedge, or you can start with the thin end. You can hold out for too much and achieve nothing, or you can assert a principle and give it force and power even though you limit its application at first. That is what _ the hon. member has in mind, I take it, in the suggested amendments of which he has spoken to the House. He is prepared to [DOT] limit his Bill so that it will be along the line that should appeal to all interests. And, the hon. member, having made that endeavour, I think it is the duty of all interests in the House to accord him support and give his measure a place on the statute-book.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: May I ask, having regard to the importance which the hon. minister attaches-and very justly- to this measure, why it is that the government does not introduce this Bill itself?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: During the last five years the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) has, each year, introduced a Bill on this subject. I had in mind introducing a Bill, or, rather, asking my colleagues to approve of my introducing a Bill dealing with the matter. On second thought I felt this would not be playing fair with the hon. member for Maisonneuve. That hon. gentleman had stood up in this House single-handed, and asked this House to adopt a principle which he believed in. And, as he had stood up in that fashion, I felt it was rather my duty to back him up rather than to try to take the credit for such a measure to myself.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Are we to understand that the Bill, with the proposed amendment, has the support of the government, and is to be put through practically as a government measure?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: If the hon. member (Mr. Vprville) makes the amendments which he has indicated to me it is his intention to make, I am quite sure he will have the backing of the government in these amendments.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Might it not be well, before we proceed further with the discussion, to have a statement as to just what these amendments are? The rest of us are not in the happy position of the Minister of Labour in knowing in advance the nature of these amendments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Dispose of this amendment first.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Yes, let us know what the amendments are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: There is a motion that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. Let that be disposed of first.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. King) has forgotten my question. I hesitate a little about asking it now. He entertained us for the most part of one hour without being interrogated, and I cannot help wondering how long it would take the hon. minister if I venture to ask a question. With all respect to my hon. friend, I may say that I have had the advantage of reading his lecture before, and of hearing it in this House once or twice. Therefore, I am sure, he will not think I am slighting him if I make no reference to his speech, as it was dealt with long ago. My question was with regard to section 2 which sets forth a great many things to which this Act shall not apply, the last being ' all agricultural work.' The Minister of Labour has had the advantage, which I have not had, of going over the evidence to which he has referred. The question I wish to put is: Would the hon. minister explain why he is in favour of a man who works on a custom house building working only eight hours a day while a man who works on a farm, at probably less than half the wages is to be allowed to work very long hours?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I mentioned that agriculture had been eliminated from the Bill because of the evidence before the committee, and the hon. member who introduced the Bill had regard, in framing the measure, to the evidence given before the committee.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
That is not my question. I put the question to the hon. minister (Mr. King), as he is the Minister of Labour. The government of which he is a member has
arrived at the conclusion that workmen working on a custom house, a government work, shall work eight hours a day. Why do they not apply that to farm labour?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Every trade is governed more or less by conditions that are peculiar to itself. It happens that in the building trades generally there is a practice governing the hours of labour, it has become a recognized thing that in the skilled trades there shall be a limited number of hours per_ day and that payment shall be on the basis of so much an hour. Of course, in the matter of fixing hours generally, this parliament has no jurisdiction, it has no jurisdiction in the matter of fixing hours of labour, either in industries or on the farm. What this Bill relates to is hours of labour on public works, that is the name of the Bill. That being so, the measure is naturally restricted to public works. As originally draft: ed, it was much wider than its title. That was pointed out to my hon. friend last year, he was shown that he had not only dealt with public works and with a variety of other things. Now he proposes to restrict his measure to public works.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I would point out that the House is in rather a peculiar position. There has not been any definite announcement by the Minister of Labour as to whether this is a government measure or not. That point ought to be made clear. It is all very well for the Minister of Labour to say that the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve should not be robbed of the honour of bringing in this Bill. But hon. members on both sides of this House know that this Bill has been brought in year after year, and practically the House has been fooled in regard to it. Now there was an admission made last year by the Minister of Labour that this was practically a government Bill. I find this in the ' Hansard ', on page 2908, in response to a question by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath), who said:
I want to know if we are to have the Bill before the House this session, as I want to vote for it.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
The intention is to get the Bill before the House as quickly as possible. Whether the government will be able to carry out that intention depends on the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Now, there is an implied admission that it is a government Bill, and I think that point ought to be clearly understood. We had the spectacle last year of a Bill that many of us considered ought to have been a government Bill, an amendment to the Criminal Code, brought in by my hon. friend from South Grey, and we had the government refusing to accept the responsibility of having the Bill defeated by its

Minister of Justice; they wished to escape the odium of having the thing lost. The Minister of Labour, to ruy mind, has practically conceded that this is a government measure. In reply to the remarks of the leader of the opposition, he has specifically stated that he has seen the amendments. Now the main principle of this Bill is that there should be an eight hour day on all government work. In the Bill as it was brought down last year the third section says:
This Act shall apply to work undertaken by the government of Canada by day labour.
That was what was meant last year. Reduced to its last analysis, that is the principle of the Bill now, and the Minister of Labour knows that is the principle. I think before this thing goes any further we ought to have it clearly understood whether the government is, or is not, at the back of this Bill.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I do not know why I have not as much right to bring in a Bill of this kind as any other hon. gentleman of this House. I am asking support from both sides of the House. I wish to say further that I do not think it is fair and just to those I represent for an hon. gentleman to make a motion at this time that the commute rise, merely to block the progress of the Bill.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Do you think it is fair to keep the amendments up your sleeve? Why don't you bring down your amendments?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I was just about producing the amendments when the motion was made. I am willing to bring down all the amendments at the proper time, and I am sure both sides of the House will be satisfied. Objection is also taken because the present Bill does not apply to farm work. Now, I have great respect for the farmers of this country, but they are not more deserving than the men who are asking for this Bill, and I want that to be well understood. The farmers have to depend upon the consumers of the city for a market for their produce. Now, Mr. Chairman, I am willing to go ahead with this measure, with the assistance of both sides of the House; but I hope, I say for God's sake, don't make this a political affair.	i	i

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I do not rise to discuss just now the merits of the Bill. As I understand it, a short time ago a motion was made that the committee rise, and before the motion is put, I desire to say a few words with regard to the time chosen for proceeding with this Bill. The Minister of Labour has shown us a volume of evidence, somewhere about two inches Mr. BURRELL.
thick, which he said was laid on every members' table only a short time ago. I confess there was one laid on my desk, but I have not had the opportunity of reading it, amongst the large number of other reports we are called upon to examine. But I do say, that since the Minister of Labour has gone to the expense of printing an enormous quantity of this report, an opportunity should be given to every member of the House, and to almost every man in the country, to read that report, before we proceed with this Bill. Go upstairs to one of the upper corridors, and what do you find? A pile of these reports containing at least four cords of printed matter. I do not know how many more are to come up from the Bureau-four cords of these reports piled there, not distributed, no man allowed to look at them, because they are, I presume, the property of the member for Maisonneuve, or the Minister of Labour. Nobody has had an opportunity of reading them, and we propose, in face of that, without the information furnished by this report, to push this Bill through. I say it is not an opportune time. I would say: Let the Bill stand until, at any rate, these reports can be distributed, until the country can get the benefit of the information that was collected last year. There is valuable information in this report, I have no doubt, information that ought to be read, valuable to a great many men, manufacturers and others, who would be deeply interested if they should all have an opportunity of reading this report, and then expressing an opinion upon it. Consequently, if there is a motion made that the committee rise, I would deem it my duty to vote for that motion, because I consider that the House is being taken at an unfair advantage by pressing this Bill through, when the members of the House, or the people of the country, have had no opportunity of reading the volumes -of evidence. There are at least, four cords of it, and perhaps more. A few moments ago I went up to measure the pile, I found there were nearly four cords perhaps five cords. And I notice from day to day as I pass by that pile, in going up to my room, that it is gradually increasing. Every day there are additions to it. In a week or two, I would not be surprised if there were five, or ten colds. I do not know what quantity the minister or the member for Maisonneuve have yet to pile up there. But this ought to be in the hands of the people, it ought to be sent out, people ought to have an opportunity of digesting that evidence; then they would be able to express an opinion on the question. I confess I am at a loss. I did, two years ago, when a Bill of a similar nature was up, express my opinion freely, in very short language. I said then, I could not see the propriety of a man on one side of

Metcalfe street, in the city of Ottawa, working on a government contract, being dismissed at 4 o'clock, and another man on the opposite side of the street working on a private building till 6 o'clock, both practically doing the same kind of work and receiving the same wages. I thought there was something unfair about it.
