I am not satisfied of the propriety of that sort of thing yet; but perhaps if I had an opportunity of reading this volume through-it would take me more than a day, it would take me two or three days-I may be able to come to a different conclusion. But at any rate, when the government of this country has gone to the expense of printing three, or four, or five, or perhaps ten cords of these volumes, they ought to he made use of, they should be put in the hands of the people to examine the evidence and judge as to the propriety of this measure I therefore feel, if it comes to a division on this question, that it will be my duty, in order to procure delay until the report can be digested, to vote that the committee rise.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the committee that dealt with this matter, I would like to say a word or two before the motion is put. In the first place, the committee sat long and performed very laborious work in collecting this evidence, which has been referred to. The evidence then collected was upon a Bill quite different in terms from the present Bill now before the House. The Bill now before the House, as proposed to be amended, from the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Verville), who introduced it, is narrower than that which was referred to the committee last session. The committee had not finished their labours before the House adjourned, but although they had made no report, they had taken and heard a very large amount of evidence. I quite agree with the opinion of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) that this Bill ought to be a government measure. It should long ago have been taken in hand by the government. It never should have been permitted to be made the political football that it has been made during the last five or six years. I also concur with the opinion expressed on this side of the House that the amendments which axe to be put in this Bill should be in the hands of the members. There should be some idea of what the amendments are to be. because the Bill is a very important one.
The evidence submitted to the committee last session fully confirmed my then opinion that an eight hour Bill is a proper and humane law to pass in this parliament in so far as it relates to the public works of the government. I am to-day of that opinion. The evidence all pointed to that conclusion, at least in my opinion, and a proper Bill framed along fair and equitable lines with that object in view will always have my support in this House. The proposal is not so drastic as some hon. members think. Some hon. members have taken objection to it on the score of it applying to agriculture. It has no application directly or indirectly to anything in connection with agriculture.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: What about the government farm?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Experimental farms are exempted under the word ' agriculture.' They appertain to agriculture. Let me point out that this Bill, as it is likely to pass this House, if I may be permitted a prediction as to what it will be when it does pass, will be a Bill applicable only to the erection by the government of public buildings throughout the country. These public buildings are erected in centres where to-day there is an almost uniform eight hour day applying to the various building trades. If you erect a public building in Toronto, or any place in Ontario, or in Winnipeg, or in any other city in the Dominion, you will find that in all these centres the eight hour day applies to the building trades, and there will be no change whatever in the hours of work on account of the passage of a law applicable to government work in these cities. When this Bill came before the House last session, from what was said in the short debate which preceded the reference of the Bill to the Select Committee, I formed the opinion that the Bill would have passed had a vote been taken then. The Bill is in a greatly modified form as it is to-day before the House, and if the House thinks it is not prepared to deal with it to-day, perhaps it is better, in the interest of all, that it should receive more consideration when the amendments, which the hon. member who introduces the Bill has indicated he intends to move, come before the committee, and altogether it seems the wiser course to leave it over for consideration. I quite agree not with all of what my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) said, but with that portion of his remarks in which he said that this evidence should be examined by the members of the House at least, and that such of the public as are interested in the matter should have an opportunity of perusing this testimony and of expressing any opinions pro and con that they may desire to express to this House. Personally, I am entirely in accord with the principle of the eight hour day as applied to labour of this class. I do not propose to go into the academic reasons for that opinion. But that is the opinion that I hold, and I will apply it to this legislation when the proper opportunity comes

for me to express an opinion before this House.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Mr' Speaker, I have not been in the House and I have not heard what has been said on this Bill, but I have my own views with regard to Bills of this kind. I think they are radically wrong. If you put any restriction upon a man's right to work for any length of time he desires I think it is wrong. Some men physically and intellectually are capable of working ten hours a day with no more injury than a man suffers who only works eight hours. If bv nature he is furnished with all the requisites to do that and he is willing to do it, whv should you restrict his rights? In mv judgment it is wrong.
But, there is another feature of such bills that we must not overlook. Go to the city of Toronto and take these public works; an armoury is being built costing $100,000 or $200,000. We always have these buildings going on and a bill like this applies to government works. They are within reasonable distance of, say, the Massey-Har-ris works where they are carrying on the business of manufacturing implements. One class of men are working eight hours a day and they are not satisfied unless they are getting the same amount of wages daily as the skilled mechanics who are working ten hours a day. The result is that you cannot get the one class of men to work ten hours while the others are only working eight houjs. Then the working hours must be made shorter to the men who are working in that line. What is the result? You say this Bill is all right because it does not apply to agriculture, but it applies to agriculture in this way that if you extend it from line to line-and this is what it aims at, because if the principle is recognized it will be changed and extended from year to year-in a short time the men in these factories that are turning out agricultural implements will be working eight hours a day. They must get the same wages for working eight hours a day that they got for working ten hours, the product of their labour is being sold to the farmer and the farmer cannot successfully carry on his work in any part of Canada by working eight hours a day. In the busy season, seeding and harvesting time, he has to work ten, twelve and very often fourteen hours a day and his family has to do the same. The farmer to-day has to pay for the product of labour that is only working eight hours a day, and which is receiving larger wages than the farm labourer is for working fourteen hours. This is a great injustice to the agricultural interests of the country. There are public w'orks scattered all over the Dominion, and when the men on the farms see the labourers on these works occupied for only eight hours a day, demoralization will follow, Mr. MACDONELL.
in the labour world and if a storm threatens and your grain and your hay are ;n danger the farmers themselves will have to work perhaps the whole night or half the night to save the crop while his hired help refuses to work because it is the hour at which other labourers stop for the day. I have frequently done that myself when a small boy on the farm, because we could not get the crop saved otherwise. This principle of an eight-hour day will soon extend from government works to other industries and although the men working in factories are driven every moment of the day under the eye of a superintendent, and although the men working on the farm have not steady labour during the day and are practically their own masters half the time, yet, when they see the employees in other industries working for only the shorter hours, the temptation will be for them to dress up at six o'clock and go into the towns and villages. Under the principle of this Bill you are compelling the farmers of Canada to work longer and longer hours to pay for the labour of men who are working shorter and shorter hours. If the men in the Massey-Harris factory are working eight hours a day where formerly they worked ten hours and continue to get the same wage for the shorter hours, it is evident that the farmer will have to pay an enhanced price for that machinery and will have to work longer hours to enable him to pay it. It is the farmers of this country who will have to stand the brunt of all this. We hear a good deal said in this House in favour of the labouring classes and we are told sometimes that we are not to speak our views, but I would be sorry to be a public man, if, when I thought a thing was wrong, I could not stand up in parliament and say so.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: It is very important that we should know exactly what the Bill is that the committee is asked to pass. The Prime Minister has said that the amendments cannot be made known to the committee while a motion that the committee rise is before the Chair. May I ask my hon. friend (Mr. Donnelly) to withdraw his motion so that w'e may learn what these amendments are?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I feel that the consideration of this Bill should not be proceeded with until we have had a reasonable time to consider what the measure is that is to be submitted to us. I will withdraw my motion that the committee rise, but I think the promoter of the Bill should be willing to postpone its consideration until the members of the committee have had a reasonable time to consider the amendments.
Motion, that the committee rise, withdrawn.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Would the Minister of Labour or the hon. member for Maisonneuve, whichever one of them is really in charge of the Bill, now state what these amendments are so that we may get an idea of the real scope of the measure.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: In fairness to the hon. member for Maisonneuve it may be said that he was proceeding to explain all the amendments when the chairman asked that they be submitted one at a time.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I must take exception to the amendments made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) who tells us it is not necessary to regulate the hours of labour. The experience of all civilized countries is that the improved condition of the labouring man has been brought about by legislation, and especially by regulation of the hours of labour. In the case of the railroads for example, it is absolutely essential that legislation should limit the hours of labour *because if the railway emnloyees are overworked the service is not efficient and there is not proper protection for life and property. Time and again it has been shown that where switchmen and telegraphers and others have had to work for unlimited hours accidents have happened and a poor service given. Again, in the interests of women and children who work in factories it has been found necessary to regulate the hours of labour. I cannot agree with the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) that this should be allowed to regulate itself. I have yet heard no good reason why the farm labourer should not be treated in this respect in the same way as other labourers in this country. Of course it will make a great difference to the farmers, but perhaps the day is coming when good farming will be done by having two shifts of labour on the one day and especially in the busy season, which I believe is already the practice in the west.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Maclean) is running a large farm himself and let me ask him if he employs his men only eight hours a day?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I do not, but if it is made the l^w I will live up to it. 1 pay $2,000 a week wages to men who work only seven hours a day and in that seven hours' work I believe they are up to their capacity. The farm labourers in our county go to work at seven and quit at six with an hour for dinner which practically makes 10 hours a day, and my opinion is that it is not quite fair that the law in this respect should discriminate *against the ordinary farm labourer. The onlv excuse for it is that it is the cus'tom in most countries. I might
say also that the improvement of the condition of agricultural labour in all countries of the world has been brought about by legislation. I may point out also that the advance in labour legislation has -been brought aibout by the representatives of labour who happened to get into parliament, and the glory of the British parliament to-day is the large representation of the working classes in it. On the other hand to the discredit of labour in the United States there is hardly a single representative of labour in the American Congress. The progress of labour legislation in England is largely due to the fact that organized labour has sent representatives to the British parliament who have gradually been able to secure legislation improving the condition of the working classes.
So that on the whole I say it is the duty of parliament to take jurisdiction over this matter to improve the conditions and probably the only way it can be done is by stepping it down or up, here and there, applying it first to one line of labour and then to another, applying it to one section of the community and then to another. It cannot be carried out as a straight movement all along the line and as an equal movement, but it can be applied very much in the way in which it is being done now. As a matter of fact, in the city of Toronto, we have largely now the eight-hour day and the general testimony is that no harm has been done to the public, something has been done to improve the condition of those who labour and in every country in which it has been tried where an attempt has been made to reduce the hours of labour, no harm has been done. But before the evil becomes too great in this country I would like to see a thorough regulation of labour, especially in the case of women and children and in the case of men engaged in unhealthy occupations. Where women and children are employed, the workshops should be better, their hours of labour should be reduced and in every way an effort ought to be made to improve the conditions particularly of those who work in what are called sweat shops, where the pay is very poor and where great disorder reigns. The evidence that has been brought out in connection with woman labour in the great city of New York, to which the magazines now are devoting great attention, goes to show the most unhealthy conditions. It is proved beyond all doubt that the treatment of the working girls in the great city of New York, where their wages do not average $4 a week, is something inhuman, that the evil is increasing and ought to be stopped and the same conditions are coming to prevail in the Canadian cities. There would be some hone for improvement in the conditions which surround the labour of women and

children if such an improvement as this could be brought about in regard to men. But I do not wish to see it applied so much to men in the first case as to women and children. There would be a much more pronounced opportunity for the enjoyment of life which the minister pointed out than there is at present so that I am quite prepared to see the eight-hour day inaugurated in this country in this limited way with the hope that it will extend and that its application may come at an early date to women and children who have to work for their living in shops.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has as usual talked on almost every imaginable question under the sun

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. HUGHES-and not one of them bearing on the question at issue. All the matters he has been discussing come within provincial jurisdiction and not under the jurisdiction of this parliament. But he did confess one thing that he, a farmer, running a large farm as he does, and having an opportunity to set an example to the people of this country without legislation, has failed to do it, has failed to give the horny handed sons of toil working for him the eight-hour day to which he says they are entitled. That is a very serious example and an indiscretion, not to use a stronger word.
This Bill concerns only government work. Why not enforce the eight-hour day on government work through the contract, as all government work should be by contract, and not burden the statute-book with this sort of thing. A number of amendments are to be proposed to this Bill, in fact I believe there are more amendments than there is Bill. Why not reprint the Bill so that we will have it before us complete? I defy either the Minister of Labour or the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-vi'.le) to stand up and make himself intelligible on these amendments to one-quarter of the members.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Just a word or two in regard to the peculiar manner of the introduction of this Bill. We have been told by the Minister of Labour, representing the government, that the chief reason why this Bill was not brought hn as a government measure was the fact that it had been introduced on several previous occasions by the present introducer. It is true that for a number of sessions of a Bill called the Eight-Hour Bill has been introduced by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville) but in every case, at some time during the session, it has disappeared. It has Mr. MACLEAN (York).
been used, as has been said, purely as a political football. This evening we have had in the House the peculiar anomaly of the Minister of Labour getting up in answer to a direct question from this side of the House, whether or not the government was prepared to- stand sponsor for this Bill, or for the principle of an eight-hour day, and making a speech with many flights of imagination, steering at times verv close to thin ice, and yet avoiding every important question asked by members of this House. We have the further peculiar fact that this Bill was introduced by a member of the House, and in introducing the Bill he tells us he is prepared with a series of amendments tcf it that will very much limit the principle asked for in the Bill. As one who is inclined to support, and who has supported the principle of the eight-hour dav, and eight-hour labour, I strongly object to the position taken both by the Minister of Labour and the member introducing the Bill. I think the course being taken is very unfair to every member-of this House. This is a question of such vital importance to all classes in this country as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) ten cords of literature have been printed at the expense of the country, evidence has been taken, collated, printed and piled in the corridors, and then we are told by the introducer that he and the Minister of Labour have talked over and discussed certain amendments on which they have agreed, and which they propose to introduce. Why did not the two>
members come together before introducing the Bill, and when they had decided on something to which the Minister of Labour could agree, and for which he would be prepared to ask his colleagues to stand sponsor, introduce the Bill in that shape, bring it before the House, so that every -member would have an equal and fair chance of seeing exactly the position the government takes and just how far this Bill limited itself in the principle for which the Minister of Labour has told us he is so anxious at this particular time. If he really believes in the principle of the eight-hour day, why should he not bring down a Bill which we would be prepared fairly to act upon, after having studied the principles and conditions that we are asked at this time to give a decision upon? That is my strong objection to the Bill. I shall not at this particular moment go into all the reasons why I believe in the principle itself, and thev are many and very strong. I have given some little attention to the report that has been brought down, and there appear to be many strong arguments why at this particular time the government of _ Canada should take some action in this matter, but I do strongly object to having a subject

of this nature, made, as has been said, a political football, and that one particular member or any member of this House, should bring in a Bill merely with the obiect of endeavouring to lead a certain class of the community to suppose they are espousing a certain principle, and then when we are asked to decide bn the merits of that Bill we are told that there will be a long series of amendments which, as has been said by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton, it will be impossible for us to properly understand. On this ground I think we should have this Bill returned to the hon. gentleman who introduced it in order that we might have those amendments printed and laid before the House and see what are the merits of this measure which those who are supporting it are offering to the people.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I wish to add my protest to that of the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) against the manner in which this Bill has come belore us. Whilst doing so, I would ask the House to bear with me while I make a few remarks on the character of the Bill in general. I represent, like my hon. friends from East Grey (Dr. Sproule), and Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), an agricultural constituency, but much as I defer to their judgment. I cannot see any reason why I should on that account oppose this legislation if I am convinced that it will work towards bettering the condition of the working man. I do not believe that agriculturists are opposed to legislation which will assist to lift higher in the scale of humanity the labouring population, and all that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville) and the twin father of the Bill, the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) have to do to engage my support is to convince me that the Bill will work towards that end and will effect some laudable object in the way of assisting generally our labouring population. I do not believe that there is a class in the community more in sympathy with the working man than those who are the best-greatest of all working men, namely, the farmers. While I would view this Bill with the utmost favour if convinced that it would really advance the interests of the labouring classes, I cannot quite agree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) as to the motive of the government in taking up this measure and forcing it through. In the first place, it does seem to me strange that though the amended Bill has a double fatherhood, it should come into the world deformed. If the government is to take the responsibility -as I understand the Minister of Labour to say it is-for the passage of this Bill in an amended form, they should have seen that it came before this House in the form in
which they intended it should pass. It does appear to me that the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has misconceived the purpose of the government. He does not see how it can be right for a labouring man working on a government contract to quit his work at four o'clock and have a labouring man across the road working on a private contract quit at six o'clock and both get the same pay. The Minister of Labour delivered to us the speech with which he has favoured the Canadian Club of some of the towns in Ontario, utilizing them for the purpose of lauding the virtues of the government to which he belongs as reflected in the Department of Labour. He points out that the sole object of the government is to improve the conditions of the working man. But what will be the result when a government contractor employs a working man at eight hours a day and pays him the same wages as the man on another contract working 10 hours a day? Should the labouring man in the one case quit work at four o'clock and in the other case quit at six, what would be the consequences? The government, who is the boss of the contractor, has the power to say to every labouring man that if he does not mark the ballot paper as he is told he will be dismissed and will thus be sentenced to work two hours a day longer than he has become accustomed to and will not get any more pay. That will be another means which the government will have in addition of the many they now enjoy of coercing the voter. When another election comes on and the Minister of Public Works and his satellites get busy employing all the men they can scratch together throughout Canada, they will have another weapon with which to coerce their votes, and I venture to suggest that this object was nearer the government's heart and more at the back of this movement than those which were described so movingly by the hon. Minister of Labour.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, in asking for this measure, were moved by any such motive 'as he imputes?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I am not referring to the motive of the Trades and Labour Congress, for I would be sorry to identify their motives with those of the government. It appears to me that we should have the amendments proposed put before the House before going further with the Bill, in order that we may be able to see whether or not, as amended, it will work out to the advantage of the labouring man. We cannot to-night, without those amendments, come to any intelligent conclusion. No doubt it has taken the Minister of Labour and the

hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville) many weeks to ponder and cogitate over those amendments, and they should not expect us to judge the whole position in a moment. The Bill should be reprinted and then referred again to the committee.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
All kinds of imputations have been attributed to the government whenever they have brought in any measure, but I never heard before that government coercion was associated with a measure for reducing the hours of the working man. My experience has always been iust the reverse. The last charge one would expect to be brought against any government bringing in a Bill to reduce the hours of labour would be that it did so for the purpose of coercing the labour vote. It is the man who extends the hours of labour who does the coercion. It seems to me that the discussion we are now having is one which should have taken place on the second reading. Both the promoter of the Bill (Mr. MacKenzie King) and the hon. gentleman who introduced it (Mr. Verville) spoke on the subject and this House unanimously accepted the principle by adopting the second reading. By that second reading the House had committed itself to the principle of the measure. It must be remembered that this Bill has been before the House three or four sessions, and that ultimately we decided to refer it to a select committee. That committee sat during some weeks last session and took evidence from all classes, and while I have had no intimation from the Minister of Labour or the hon. gentleman who presented the 'Bill as to what the proposed amendments are to be, I understand that they are based on the evidence received before that select committee and intended to remove the objections there made and meet what appeared to be the view of the majority as shown by the witnesses who came before that committee. If the government is prepared to support a measure introduced by a private member, with the amendments suggested as the result of the deliberations of the select committee, personally I can see no objection to our taking up that-a measure developed as the result of the intelligence of the select committee-measure with its amendments at present. I do not see that it matters whether the Bill is presented by a private member or not. There would be still further ample opportunity to reconsider these amendments before the third^ reading. Let the Bill be considered now in committee, let the amendments proposed be discussed by the committee and inserted in the Bill, and let the Bill, as amended, be reprinted, and, having accepted the principle, we can give the details every consideration they require before the third reading is passed.
Mr. MEKtHEN.
I could take up the time of the House telling how much has been done for the working classes of other countries by legislation of this kind. But I assume that many hon. members know as much about that as I do. In any case, this is not an opportune time for an address of that description. But I would remind the House that the employers of the labour affected by this Bill are in this House. The government are the employers, and other hon. members are representatives, of the public. This Bill has no reference to agricultural labour or to factories; to cover these would be to encroach upon the jurisdiction of the provinces. The Bill simply says that in certain classes of labour-and I understand that it is confined to the construction of public works under the Dominion government-men shall not be called upon to work more* than eight hours a day and that the day labourer employed by the government should be in the same position. I under-i stand these are to be the provisions of the amended Bill. I can say, as a member from British Columbia, that, if this is to be the Bill, then the Bill will not conflict with any public interest in my province. Legisla-j tion already existing in British Columbia^ provides that all the principal trades to be affected by this Bill are confined by legislation and by trades union agreements to the principle of an eight-hour-day. The rule of an eight-hour-day in certain employments is worldwide and has been acknowledged by every civilized country. I am glad to hear it stated in this House; that the government has arrived at the conclusion that the men employed under contract for the government in certain* capacities shall not be expected to work for more than eight hours a day. I think the committee could well proceed with the' Bill, dealing with the amendments as they are presented. Then, after the Bill is reprinted the House will have an opportunity to consider the whole measure. Instead of reflecting upon the Minister of Labour or upon the government for not having taken charge of this measure, I cannot see that it makes any difference except to the member who wants an excuse for not supporting it. I do not see what difference it makes, if the principle of the Bill be sound, whether it is introduced by the government or by the hon. member for Maisonneuve. If the principle of a Bill is correct, for my part, I am prepared to support it whether it is moved by a private member or by the government. If these amendments are inaccord with the evidence given before the committee by witnesses from all over the country, I think the government is reasonable in supporting that legislation. And

I shall be well pleased to contribute my vote in favour of the eight-hour principle which has been acknowledged in England, Germany, Australia and in several of the provinces of this country as a reasonable principle. And I am pleased to know that the government is ready to support* that principle.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
At present the question before the Chair is as to clause 2. So long as the motion to rise was before the committee, the whole ques->
Cion was open, and it appeared to be the strong desire of the committee to discuss the whole subject. I do not wish to stand in the way of that continuing, but I think it my duty to remind the committee that the subject under discussion is section 2.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) said he did not see any difference between having the Bill in charge of a private member or having it in charge of the government. I think it must be plain to every hon. member that there is in this all the difference between the success and the failure of the Bill. I would ask the Minister of Labour whether it is the intention of the government to facilitate the passing of the Bill to its third reading in this House. Because, hon. members know perfectly well that this is the last Thursday to be devoted to private members' work, and very few facilities will be given this Bill to be passed if it remains in the hands of a private member. And I would call attention to the fact also that the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Verville) has had several opportunities to move the second reading and has delayed the measure repeatedly in order that opportunity might be given the Minister of Labour to promulgate his views in sympathy with the Bill without any real intention of passing the measure. I am not opposed to any measure that will alleviate the condition of the labouring classes. But we must remember that the effect of this measure must be to increase enormously the cost of public works. And, as the farming community form one-third of our population, that increased cost will fall mainly in the agricultural classes. Representing, as I do, an agricultural constituency, I am bound to oppose this very much.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
The Bill as it appears on the Order Paper is a public Bill, and it seems to me immaterial whether it is presented by a private member or by the government. The Bill will iconsecrate the principle of an eight-hour day for labour, and I think, should have the sympathy of every member of this House who is in favour of the labouring classes. I would point out that this Bill will apply to government works alone. Let me give an instance. In
the city of Hull, immediately across tne river from Ottawa, there are a great number of labourers employed in the departments of this government. These poor labourers have to leave their homes, in many cases, at six o'clock in the morning in order to reach their work at the time appointed by the government for work to begin. If they wished to have breakfast before leaving their homes, they must get up at 5 o'clock, and many of them have to get up at 4 and half past four in the morning. Hon. gentlemen must admit that in the cold winter months it is unreasonable to say that these poor labourers who have to go perhaps three or four miles from their homes in the early hours of the morning, should not be given a fair opportunity to enjoy some of the luxuries which the richer classes enjoy at every hour in the day.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Do not these same conditions apply to men working for private individuals?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Yes, they certainly do, and I would be glad to see all classes of the labouring population in this country given the same facilities and the same advantages which the hon. member for Maison-neuve proposes that we should give to men labouring on public works. But at the present moment, we cannot legislate for other classes. We can only legislate upon matters affecting the government of this country. Therefore, I heartily approve, as I did last session, of the principle of an eight-hour-day Bill, and I hope it will go through.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman who introduced this Bill, made a speech on the second reading, saying that he was going to introduce some amendments. We supposed those amendments would be put before us, because the Minister of Labour said that on the strength of those amendments, he intended to support the Bill. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) says he knows what those amendments are, and he is prepared to support them. But we on this side of the House, know nothing about them.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I never said I had seen those amendments.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Then the hon. gentleman has great faith in the member for Maisonneuve, if he is willing to support this Bill before he has seen the amendments, and does not know anything about them, according to his own statement. I am not like my hon. friend. I want to know what I am doing, I want to understand the language of the Bill that I am helping to enact. I did not experience such treatment in regard to a Bill that I introduced. I had a Bill on the Order Paper, and it had to stand, because the Minister of Railways was not in the House,

although the government could not object to it and its merits. The hon. member for Maisonneuve has been introducing legislation of this kind for four or five years past, to my knowledge, but never attempting to get it to a second reading. Now he brings it in at half past nine o'clock on the evening of the last day he can do so, before parliament takes its Christmas recess. We have not had an opportunity of studying the Bill, we have not seen the amendments, and yet the hon. member for Maisonneuve asks us for God's sake not to stop this Bill. When did he think it was necessary to make that prayer to the Almighty for the first time in regard to this legislation?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I asked the House not to make a political affair of it.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
What has the hon. gentleman been doing himself ? What has he been doing with this Bill for the last five years ? Talk about making a political question of it ! I do not know whether I am in favour of his Bill or not, because I do not know what the Bill is. The hon. member for Nanaimo says that the principle can be well understood before we reach the third reading, and yet he found fault with us for not objecting to the principle of the Bill before the second reading. What chance have the labouring men of this country got with a government that acts on such logic as that ? What I would suggest is that the hon. member for Maisonneuve send through the post office to every member of this House by to-morrow a copy of his amendments, so that we may have a chance to consider them before the Christmas holidays, and that after consulting with our constituents, we may come back here, prepared to give the Bill an intelligent consideration. None of us had any idea that this Bill was coming up tonight. We have had no opportunity of considering the amendments, which it is admitted, are of so much importance that they involve the principle of the Bill. The general principle of the Bill should be known before the Bill leaves the com mittee. The Minister of Labour admitted that his object is to get in the thin end of the wedge, and to cause everybody to go in for an eight hour day; other hon. gentlemen support the Bill, because they think it does nothing of the kind. If the object of the Minister of Labour is to coerce the rest of the people of Canada into adopting an eight-hour day, I am not with him. This is still a free country, and he has no business to try to coerce the provincial legislatures to make laws that they might not be disposed to make. If however, as the hon. member for Nanaimo suggests, the Bill is only to apply to government work, that might be a different thing, and Mr. LANCASTER.
I might support it. But I say that we ought not to pass section 2, until we have these amendments before us. Surely it is not using too strong an expression to say that the opposition in this House, at all events, are being taken by the throat tonight in regard to this legislation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I think I ought to call the attention of the committee to the fact that section 2 is before the committee. If there is a motion to rise and report and ask leave to sit -again, of course, there might be a discussion. But, at present I have to restrict it to section 2.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
With reference to the observation that this Act is not to be applied to the agricultural work I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to section 2 in connection with clause 5. Section 5 says in effect that :
No labourer, workman or mechanic in the employ of the government shall be permitted to work more than eight hours in any one calendar day.
The Minister of Labour said that the object of this Bill is to set an example in the matter of progressive labour legislation. This clause 5 says in effect that none of the labourers, mechanics or workmen employed on any of the agricultural farms belonging to the Dominion government shall be permitted to work for more than eight hours a day, while the poor agricultural labourer across the line is liable to be bound down from daylight to dark. I want to know if it is the intention of the government to enforce a rule of this kind with respect to men employed on the model agricultural farms while at the same time no provision is made for the poor agricultural labourer across the line.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Is there any objection to stating what the amendments are?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Not at all. Why should we not have them? In view of the position taken by the Chair, we cannot. according to the strict rules of parliament, allow any general discussion on the subject unless a motion is made that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. That will give an opportunity to my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) to state what the amendments are, and therefore, I beg to move that the committee rise.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I have no objection to stating what the amendments are. I have nothing to hide from this House. I propose to amend section 2, paragraphs (a) and (c), by striking out the words ' in the open market ', and paragraph (b) by adding the words ' or if war is appre-

hended.' Sections 4 and 5, are to be stricken out altogether.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: How much will there be left of the Bill?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I will answer my hon. friend when I get through. It is proposed to amend section 6 as follows. After the word ' contract ' in line 19 insert the words ' hereafter made for the erection, remodelling, construction, or repair of any public building.' In line 25, strike out the words ' or permitted.' In line 26, after the words ' more than ' insert the words * forty-eight hours in any one week or where employment is for less time than one week.' In line 27, the following words are to be added to section 6 ' additional hours, if worked, shall be classified as overtime and paid for at the rate of not less than time and a quarter.' I will read the whole clause.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman read the clause as he proposes it?	.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
The clause as amended will read:-
Every contract hereafter made for the erection, remodelling, construction or repair of any public building of which the government of Canada is a party, which may involve the employment of labourers, workmen or mechanics, shall contain a stipulation that no labourer, workman or mechanic in the employ of the contractor, sub-contractor or other person doing or contracting to do the whole or any part of the work contemplated by the contract, shall be required, except in case of extraordinary emergency, to work upon or in connection with the work contracted for, more than forty-eight hours in any one week, or where employment is for a less time than one week, eight hours in any one calendar day; additional hours if worked shall be classified as over-time, and paid for at a rate of not less than time and a quarter.
Then clauses 7 and 8 are to be stricken out.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Oh.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Hon. members need not be surprised.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: We are not.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Neither is the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Do you want to hear any more to-night?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Is that all the amendments you have to propose?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
There is something else. I propose to substitute the following for clause 7.-
7. Any officer or agent of the government of Canada or any contractor or sub-contractor
thereof who violates any of the provisions of this Act shall be liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding two hundred dollars and costs or to imprisonment for not more than six months, or to both fine anl imprisonment.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman add a clause stating who will enforce the law if it is broken?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The law will be enforced.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: You were not listening to the discussion this afternoon if you think that.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The working people will see that it is enforced as they have seen that the fair wage clause is enforced. Now, Mr. Chairman, I have given all the details and I don't see why we cannot proceed with the Bill. I have nothing to hide.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I am surprised that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Ver-ville) has introduced to the House such an important Bill in such a manner. The hon. gentleman knows that I am in favour of labour legislation to benefit the workingmen, and that I am especially in favour of an eight-hour day Bill, but the Bill he presents to-night is a thing of such shreds and patches that you cannot make head or tail out of it. Some twelve years ago, long before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Verville) had a seat in this House, I myself proposed an eight-hour day Bill, but 1 found I was a little ahead of the times, and the fact that I introduced such a Bill was one of the main factors which led to the Hon. Charles
H.	Hyman defeating me in 1900. But, since then, people have changed their minds with regard to legislation for the benefit of the working people. It is a rather curious coincidence that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Verville) who introduces this Bill, travelled all the way from Montreal, during one of my elections, and brought with him the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) to endeavour to defeat me, although, as I have said I was one of the first in Canada to propose the eight-hour day legislation.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: What kind of a canui-date did you have against you?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: A labour candidate.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Exactly.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Well, I was just as much of a labour candidate as he was, and I had worked all my life at least equally as hard and quite as respectably as he did in the interest of the working people, and the people of London I am thankful to say showed their appreciation of that by returning me to this House. When the hon. member for Maisonneuve honoured London with his presence he called a meeting, and

I think he only got 35 people to attend. Then they resorted to securing a brass band and I am told they had about 120 people following it boys and all included. As I have said, Mr. Chairman, things have changed since I had the privilege of introducing an eight-hour Bill in this House. One of the principal manufacturers in London told me a short time ago that he had voluntarily adopted the eight-hour rule in his establishment, with the result that he got better work done than formerly under the longer hours, and so satisfied is he with the system that he would not change it now. 1 refer to Mr. McCormick, who is engaged in the biscuit business.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Does he make good biscuits?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Yes, he makes the best biscuits in Canada; but of course I must give the Minister of Customs credit for making good biscuits too. Mr. McCormick is perfectly satisfied with the eight-hour a day system and Mr. McCormick is a gentleman who would not make that statement to me unless he believed it were true. Tonight I have heard a good deal said about the agricultural community and about the long hours they have to work. That may be all true during the harvest season, but there is no man working on a farm who works more than ten hours a day and he does not work that long all the year round. During the harvest season they have long hours on the farm, but for the remaining eight months of the year they get up in the morning and feed their cattle and they have nothing to do until feeding time comes again at night. I really believe that the people working on farms do not work more than eight hours a day on an average all the year round. I think the men working on the farms work long enough, but I object to their position being used as an argument why the people working in the different industries throughout the Dominion should be compelled to work long hours.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
If the suggestion I made last session had been adopted we would not be to-night discussing this Bill as we are doing. One strange thing in connection with this Bill and the oration we had from the Minister of Labour is, that at the outset the Minister of Labour told the leader of the opposition that when he knew what the amendments which the hon. member (Mr. Verville) was going to propose were, he would be able to say whether the government would approve of the Bill, but a moment later he was compelled to admit that he knew all about these amendments in advance, if they had not been framed by him. There has been a good deal of shuffling between the Minister of Labour and the member for Maisonneuve in connection with this Bill. It reminds me of the old time Irish Mr. BEATTIE.
jig. When they got two pretty good dancers and it was hard to tell the difference between the two they selected a jig that the two could not dance together, and so each of them took turn about on the floor just as the Minister of Labour and the member for Maisonneuve are doing to-night, and you have to keep your eyes open to see which one of them is dancing best in order to determine which of them will get the glory. But, the Minister of Labour has been five years working at a measure of this kind and as he has had all the glory during that period he things he can give a little of it to the member for Maisonneuve to-night. The Minister of Labour has for five years been well fed on glory, and by this time, between the Minister of Labour and the member for Maisonneuve, I think the working men of Canada are getting pretty well fed on this Bill. Time will tell whether there is any sincerity in these hon.* gentlemen opposite with regard to this legislation, and when the resolution of my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Maddin) comes before the House we will be able to determine where the sincerity is. While these gentlemen opposite are pressing this Bill through the House of Commons tonight in a hurry, I believe we will find there is a string to'it, and that when it goes to another Chamber the string will be pulled and the Bill slaughtered. I am in favour of this Bill.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: How do you know what it is?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Well, I was in favour of the Bill when it started out, but it has got rather mixed up lately, and it is hard to tell what it means. It reminds me of a great prohibitionist who, on one occasion, attended a banquet, and he was favoured with a drink called a cocktail, and on being asked how he liked it, he said he did not take very much to the cherry, but he liked the spirit in which it was given. I cannot say I think very much of the Bill now, but I like the spirit in which it is given. I do say, that we should have taken this course last year, in place of putting this Bill off and having a committee, piling up cords of this kind of thing, all we required to do, was to take up the Bill and deal with it. We only needed to keep off as many lawyers as possible and the Minister of Labour would have been enabled to produce a good Bill, some of us farmers and working men could have worked out a Bill that every one could understand. Instead of that we said:	We
will waste another vear and get all this matter. If that testimony is any good, we should read it.' I do not require to read it, I made up my mind last year that what we ought to do, and wanted to do, was simply to pass a Bill that would give an eight-hour day on all public works un-

der construction by the government or un der contract by contractors to the government, that is all public works, public buildings, canals, &c., under construction. It seemed to me very easy and very simple, if we meant business, to put such a Bill on the statute-book, as would cover exactly what we desire and what the workingmen of this country desire, it is all very well for men to get up and say we do not want to put a Bill on the statute-book to force men not to work more than eight hours a day; they are asking for it, the workingmen have been asking for this Bill for a long time. The hon member foi London (Mr. Beattie), has said that 12 years ago, he moved such a Bill, and he was the right kind of man to do so, because he meant business when he moved it, and if he had had encouragement, he would have put it through. Lawyers neai me, say it would take them two or three weeks to fully grasp the meaning of this Bill with the proposed amendments. We have already voted for the principle, we adopted the principle of the eight-hour day on public works in this Dominion at the last session, and why should we be bamboozled about this thing now?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Then why don't you let it go through?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: It might go through you.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: We would have a hard time to get it through you.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: It might take longer to go through you than it would to go through me, but it would not take you so long to go through anything else. I am in accord with the principle of the Bill this year as I was last year; my only fear in regard to it, is that I do not believe there is a sincere effort behind it on the part of the Minister of Labour or the government or the member for Maisonneuve, who moved it. However, if, as the session advances the hon. member will prove to me that he means business and will see that the Bill goes through, I will be glad to apologize to him for what I have said, and I shall be glad to see the day when we will have taken this long step in the right direction. I am quite in accord with the references that have been made by the Minister of Labour to the working people, and the care we should give them.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
When a Bill, somewhat similar to this one, was before the House last session, I expressed myself as in ac cord with the principle of that enactment, and voted against its being referred to a special committee, urging that the matter be taken up in Committee of the Whole at that time, and that such amendments as were necessary, should there be introduced. Had my counsel been followed a Bill substantially the same as this 46
would have been in operation for the last six or seven months. However, the Bill found its way to that committee. For some ten years now, we have had a Department of Labour, which was created at first under the Department of the Postmaster General, and many people in Canada are very anxious to know for just what purpose this department exists, for when the only important piece of labour legislation since 1908, came before this parliament, a Bill respecting the hours of labour on public works, it was referred to a committee. For what purpose? To gather statistics, facts and figures with regard to the hours of employment on public works in other countries and with regard to the hours of labour in different employments in other countries. Eventually, of+er the matter had gone to a committee, after this volume of evidence had been elicited from the Manufacturers' Association, from employers of labour, from labour unions, a commissioner was sent to gather still further information with regard to the matter. I submit that the Department of Labour has failed utterly in the purpose for which it was inaugurated if, .after ten years, with the present Minister of Labour acting as deputy, travelling throughout every civilized country in the world, and studying economic and labour conditions, it becomes necessary in the opinion of the government to submit a trifling little Bill with five sections in it, to a special committee of this House, which was obliged to sit for 19 days and to issue a volume of evidence such as has been submitted.
I would like to feel quite certain that/ the government is sincere in their endea-( vour to pass such legislation. Whether i1) pass in the form of this Bill or whether' the amendments be adopted is neither here nor there, but I would like to feel some assurance that the government are sincere in their effort to make this Act or the substance of it, part of the law of this country. In 1906 there appeared on the Order Paper of this House a Bill entitled: an Act' respecting the hours of labour on public works. Its title appeared on the Order Paper during the sessions of 1907, 1908 and 1909. We have had it again this year, and I would like to point out that during all these years, it has appeared in the name of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville). The hon. gentleman was president of the Trades and Labour Council of Canada and was elected, not as a Liberal or Conservative, but as a representative of labour. During all those years however during which this Bill was before the House, to what extent did he exhibit activity with regard to it. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. King) to-night, after he had expressed his sym-



pathy with the Bill and endorsed its principle, why he did not adopt it as a government measure? In reply, we were treated to a demonstration of heroics by the Minister of Labour. He became very tender-hearted all at once and fair play and equity fairly beamed from him. He said it would not be fair to the hon. member for Maisonneuve, to whom the labouring classes were under obligations, it would not be playing the game fair, if the government should take the matter out of his hands, but that now the government was prepared to adopt it. Within a few minutes afterwards, when the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) was making his speech before this committee, he raised his hands and said: For God's sake do not drag politics into this discussion. Now I want to deal with that prayer that went up to heaven to-night and test the sincerity of the mover of the Bill. On September 22, 1909, the Trades and Labour Council met in the city of Quebec, and Mr. O'Donohue, parliamentary solicitor of that body, then delivered his preliminary report. From that report I intend to make a few quotations for the benefit of members of this committee and particularly for the benefit of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville):-
Mr. Verville introduced a Bill to provide for an eight-hour day on government contracts. The Bill stood while I was endeavouring to prevail upon the government to make it a government Bill and thus insure its passage into law.
There was then no pretense on the part of the parliamentary solicitor, who was making his report to the Trades and Labour Council that the government was sympathetic with the hon. member for Maisonneuve and did not want to rob him of any glory. But what further do we find in this report, and mark you, this is a report which was read in the presence of the man who prays to God that politics will not be dragged into the discussion. Mr. O'Donohue further says:-
I further endeavoured to secure enough supporters to at least make certain of a division on a second reading.
Mr. Chairman, I went to the trouble of asking personally sixty-seven members who sit to the left of the Speaker, and I was assured that not one of them was ever approached, either by the solicitor of the Trades and Labour Council or the hon. member for Maisonneuve, and asked to support this Bill. The report goes on to say:-
The absence of the Hon. Mr. King and illness of in the family of the then Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mr. Lemieux, were other causes that contributed to the delay. Finally Mr. MADDIN
when it was determined to push the Bill it had become tied up on the Order Paper, and the only thing that could be done was to have the order discharged so that a discussion could be had on the merits.
So that in spite of the appeal to heaven that politics might not be dragged into the thing, we have the solicitor of the council making this further report.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am willing to accept my own responsibility, but I am not an officer of that organization, now.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: Were you then?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I was.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I turn to another page of the report:-
Quebec, September 22, 1909.
Third Day-Morning Session.
President Verville called the convention to order at 9 a.m.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I did not say that I was not a member then. I acknowledged like a man that I was. But I say that now I am not an officer of it any longer.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
I am not surprised that after the members of that council ' discovered what was going on in the House, the hon. gentleman should no longer be an officer of that association. The report goes on to say:-
Mr. Verville presented the resolution in a very forcible and able speech, his efforts being ably seconded by Mr. C. A. Turcotte, Nicolet, Mr. Jos. Girard, Chicoutimi and Saguenay, Mr. J. D. Taylor, New Westminster, and Mr. Crosby, Halifax. Hon. Mr. Lemieux said lie found that there were some very grave difficulties in the way.
I pass over part of the report. I am only reading it in so far as it bears on the prayer that went from the hon. gentleman s lips to-night, but I doubt if the prayer on his lips and the meditations in his heart would harmonize very well:-
The Hon. Mr. Lemieux said he found there were some very grave difficulties in the way. In nearly all states of the American commonwealth there exists, he said, an eight-hour law, but it has been limited to certain industries. As drawn, he would not support the Bill, but he declared that it was legislation worth studying and investigating. An eight-hour law on government contracts, he argued, would be in conflict with provincial legislation as it stands.
Apparently at this council, the parliamentary solicitor was apologizing for the views expressed by the then Minister of Labour (Mr. Lemieux). But the report contains a further apology for the Minister of Labour of that date:-
It is quite apparent that the Hon. Mr. Lemieux was not able to give the subject the study it deserved or he would not have spoken

as lie did. In the first place, the delegates will recall that on several occasions the hon. gentlemen declared himself fully in accord with our demand in this regard and stated that all we had to do was to convert his colleagues. If the hon. gentleman thinks the Bill is class legislation, he cannot fairly he in favour of it, whether in its present form or any other.
Then, in order that this committee may-further appreciate how determined were these gentlemen-the then president of the Trades and Labour Council (Mr. Verville) and its solicitor (Mr. O'Donahue)-for God's sake to keep this thing out of politics. Mr. O'Donahue concludes his report as follows :-
While the opposition jeered at the honesty of purpose of Mr. Verville, it is worthy of note that the Hon. Mr. Borden did not speak in favour of the Bill, nor did others of the opposition except those mentioned above.
Suddenly in the last sentence, the measure becomes a Bill again. First, it was a Bill, then a resolution, and finally a Bill again We have here an instance of a president of the Trades and Labour Council (Mr. Verville) coming into this House as a labour representative and then following the government as servilely as its most abject supporter. We find him placing on the Order Paper year after year a measure which he does not bring before the House, which he does not introduce into it, and then going back with his parliamentary solicitor at his elbow convening delegates from all over Canada, and conveying to them such false and glaring misrepresentations as I have read-misrepresentations bristling with partisanship and politics from beginning to end-and then we have this hon. gentleman raising his hands to heaven and exclaiming for God's sake do not drag politics into this discussion.
When this Bill was before this House last session, or a Bill similar to it, I expressed myself in sympathy with its object. I do not agree that this measure in any way comes into conflict with our farming population. I do not think the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) or the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) need express any undue anxiety as to the toiling masses who till the soil. They seem to think that the working hours of the farmer are much too long. And, as I recall his words, the hon. member for Fron-' tenac said that the farmer does more hard work in a given time than the man of any other class. Perhaps he does. But whether he does or not it is certainly true that he takes longer rests and takes them more frequently than the ordinary labourers in the industrial centres. There is no occasion to be exercised over the farming population. Those of the west, we know, in seed-time and in harvest work very hard.
461	'
But it was stated in the debate on the resolution regarding the chilled meat trade that cattle raising and feeding is dwindling to little or nothing; and we were assured by one hon member that some of the farmers kept only four or five head of cattle. What do they do in winter? Why, they spend their winters in Florida or California. Almost every farmer owns his automobile. And when they have garnered their wheat and taken it to the elevators, they think nothing of coming to Ottawa in car-loads to present their demands. But the men from the industrial centres of Canada would find it difficult, indeed-the men who work ten hours a day in the mines or workshops-to come before this House when even this important legislation is engaging our attention. They would find it difficult to fill even one second-class car from the maritime provinces, for instance. The conditions of the two classes are different. The farmer is his own boss; he is independent. And, when his crops are in, with a box of McDonald's twist and a chest of tea, and a good woodpile outside the door, he can sit at his own fireside and put in a reasonably soft time, as most of them do. I have not that peculiar symnathy with the farming classes that would lead me to oppose this Bill on the ground that it might conflict with the interests of agriculture, and make the people dissatisfied with the farm. There is little possibility of the farmers of the west or of Ontario coming to the coal mines of Nova Scotia because the hours of lab,our there are shorter. They prefer the open air and to be their own masters. There is little likelihood of their going into the workshops of the cities because the hours are shorter. And, as they find in the industrial centres such a ready market for the products of the farm, there must be that bond of sympathy between the producer on the farm, and the consumer in the town that would harmonize interests and cause the farmers to sympathize with a Bill of this kind, especially when it does not interfere with them or their interests.
There is one other reason why, I submit, the government having expressed themselves in sympathy with the spirit of this Act, should assume the responsibility of it. It has been urged, and so hinted in this report of the Trades and Labour Council by their parliamentary solicitor, that the passage of this Bill would be a guarantee to the toiling masses that on government works labour would be reduced to eight hours a day. On the other hand, the government would have to accept the responsibility of legislation of that kind. I have no doubt that a perusal of the evidence-I have not had time to peruse it all-taken on a similar Bill last winter will disclose strong protests from the manufacturers and

the contractors. And I presume that the government, through their Minister of Labour, are pandering to the labour organizations of the Dominion, expressing their sympathy with the Bill, but avoiding the responsibility of promoting the Bill in this House, because this will leave them in a position to sav to the labourers: We have shortened your hours of labour from ten hours to eight hours, and to the manufacturers: It was not a government measure, but was introduced bv the member for Maisonneuve and enough members on either side voted for it to carry it, but we are not responsible for it. In fact, the government is plaving heads I win, tails you lose. They hope to cover themselves with glory if the Bill goes through in its present form and with its present mover, and, on the other hand, they are prepared to repudiate any responsibility for it. This must be quite evident, I think, when they 1 refuse to make this a government measure. There is a further consideration. If the Department of Labour, which was created for the purpose of looking after the labouring and manufacturing interests of Canada, has any sympathy with this Bill and deems it expedient that expression should be given in the form of a statute to the principle involved in the Bill, I submit that it becomes the duty of the government to express that opinion in the form of a Bill and submit it to this House. They should not leave it to the hon. member for Maisonneuve. who is inexperienced-I am sure he will not take any offence at mv saying so- in drafting measures to be submitted to parliament. It is the dutv of the government, if they approve the spirit of the Act, to prepare a Bill expressing their views and submit it to the House, and not have Bill after Bill introduced session after session, no two Bills alike, and now the Bill and its amendments coming in together and all emanating from the mover of the Bill. This is surely very singular and very anomalous. The whole thing could be obviated bv the Minister of Labour assuming the responsibilities of his office and taking hold of this subiect in the proper manner. This is onlv a short and simple Bill, and, surelv, with his ten years' experience throughout the civilized world and his study of economic and labour conditions, the hon. Minister of Labour, in an afternoon, could prepare a Bill covering his views on the subiect of hours of labour on public works.
