speechtext:
I think I am within the mark in saying that we have had exhibited here to-night the most extraordinary performance on the part of a minister of the Crown and leader of a great movement that has ever been witnessed within these walls. Before proceeding to refer in detail to the reasons which have led me to that conclusion, I Mr. MADDIN.
would like to recall an incident of last year in connection with a Bill of similar title. That Bill was referred by this House, as some of us thought and said at the time, to a committee in the hope that that committee would strangle it and that nothing more would be heard of it. The committee considered the Bill at very great length. They made a report of several hundred pages entirely favourable, as I gather, to the principle of an eight-hour day in government employment. One would think that the Minister of Labour, having presided as chairman over the deliberations of that committee, and having had as his colleague the hon. member for Maisonneuve who has presented this Bill, if he thinks this Bill is in the interest of labour, would have conferred with the hon. gentleman who presented the Bill, and would at least have given us some idea as to whether he intends to give the Bill the endorsement of the government so as to ensure its passage through this House. Nothing of the kind occurred, however. The member for Maisonneuve has been allowed to go on this year as in the past, without any assistance from the Department of Labour, and when he brings in the Bill, a Bill which I have every reason to believe is the product of the Trades and Labour Congress, or if not, is the result of deliberation on the part of the leaders of labour in this country- when he brings in that Bill in his name, and offers it to this House, the Bill is deliberately strangled by the Minister of Labour, who should have helped him to prepare a reasonable measure. Now. I refer to this as an extraordinary spectacle, and I wish to call attention to the evidence. We have here a Bill submitted as to which we were asked to vote the affirmation of the principle, as we did on the second reading, providing a large measure of restriction in reference to labour on government works. So great was the confidence, apparently, of hon. gentlemen on the government side of the House in the integrity of the Minister of Labour, a confidence voiced by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) who at one time sat in this House as a labour member himself, and who said to us a little while ago : I have an abiding faith in the integrity of the Minister of Labour-

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: No, I was referring to the member for Maisonneuve.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I accept the explanation of the member for Nanaimo, he had not an abiding faith in the integrity of the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend's capacity for misconstruction is being illustrated. It is a very unfair statement for my hon. friend to make. I stated

that I had an abiding faith in the hon. member for Maisonneuve that he was prepared to make reasonable amendments. 1 made no reference whatever to the Minister of Labour.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: May I ask what the hon. gentleman's question is?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
Yes, if the minister likes to answer my question I

will sit down. I am afraid, however, that the Minister of Labour is a little weary. He arose just now and I would be delighted to sit down and let him answer the question.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I was asking the hon. gentleman what the question was.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: My question is: What is the object or application of section 3 of the Bill as it now stands before us?

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: As I understand, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Verville) intends to have the eight-hour day principle apply to day labour performed by the government and also to contracting.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
It
seems that I have paid too high a compliment to the intelligence of the Minister of Labour. If the minister had not consented to strike out section 5 then the answer wdiich he has just now made to the committee might be accepted as having a grain of sense in it. But, with the disappearance of section 5 from this Bill any pretense of sense in the contention that by any possibility section 3 as it now stands can have any meaning in this Bill has completely disappeared.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: The hon. member is hardly fair. The Bill has been presented in a certain form. Some amendments have been suggested to it, but it may be that the amendments that have been suggested will necessitate further amendments to carry out the original intention of the promoter of the Bill.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext:
That is one sentence in which 1 do agree with the Minister of Labour-that the amendments which he has permitted his colleague in this work of labour reform to propose to this House do necessitate several other amendments and that to which I call attention is one. I am reminded of the statement by the minister early this evening that he had conferred with the introducer of this Bill in respect to the amendments.
I understood from his statement then that the amendments were his own work.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I do not know that I gave any reason for that understanding.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: I am bound to take the minister's statement that he gave no reason for that understanding. It is true that there was a good deal associated with his explanation of this Bill that I entirely fail to understand. Now, not to delay the committee, I wish to state that I am in favour of the principle of an eight-hour day on government works and not only the principle but the practice. I also agreed with the Minister of Labour when, with characteristic eloquence, he dilated upon the advisability of the gov- >

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.
speechtext: ernment being a model employer of labour. I agreed with the sentiment he then expressed that the government should be a model employer. It is because I think the government should be a model in this respect that I feel thankful when a Bill of this character does come before the House because I am convinced that the experience of eight hours a day labour on government works will prove so satisfactory as to lead to a general extension of the principle. But while I admired that statement of the minister I was disaonointed that in connection with works directly controlled by the .government he proposed to exempt labourers from the benefits of the operation of this Act. We have a number of experimental farms directly controlled by the government as to which it is quite practicable to enact that as a general rule at least there shall be 8 hours a day labour. Yet we find them expressly exempted. We have a number of penitentiaries directly under the control of the government not competing with any other interests in the country. The hours of labour there are 12, as I understand it. To me it is gross inhumanity that these employees of the government should be called upon to work these hours. I was disappointed that section 5 as it existed in this Bill did not cover that class of labour. I think it should. I would affirm, in conclusion, that I am in favour of the principle and practice of the 8 hour day on government works. I am also in favour of the proposition that this committee shall rise and report progress, because I think it is absolute folly to attempt to go on with the Bill in the shape in which it now stands before us.

maintopic: HOURS OF LABOUR ON PUBLIC WORKS.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Not at all; my hon. friend the Minister of Labour says that in this Bill, like all other Bills, one amendment might suggest another.
